messages.content: It's really cool to walk along Pingjiang Road tonight. The autumn leaves look nice with the lanterns.

I totally agree. Well, the air is crisp, and you know, the old houses make the whole area feel very special. I'm actually thinking about trying the local weaving workshop nearby. Have you ever considered learning silk weaving?
I have seen some silk patterns at my company, but I didn't think I could do it myself.

You can, if you are willing to practice. In some sense, the techniques passed down from my grandfather are still used today. He taught me how to prepare the silk threads before we start weaving. It takes time, but it's worth it.
That sounds hard. My job as an engineer is very busy. I work until late every day.

I understand that pressure. Honestly, balancing a full-time job with evening classes is tough. However, many people in Suzhou manage it by attending workshops on weekends only. If you start now, you'll see progress over time.
Maybe next weekend. I want to see my family's old loom at home first.

That is a great idea. You know, preserving family heirlooms is important in our culture. My own family has a wooden loom that my great-grandgrandmother used. It was kept in the storage room for years, but now we take it out to show visitors.
Oh, that is special. Did your grandfather fix the machine?

Actually, he repaired most of the parts. He knew how to adjust the tension of the thread manually. If the machine was broken, he would fix it without using modern tools. It shows his deep knowledge of the craft.
I feel sad that younger people don't want to learn these old skills anymore.

It's true. Many young people prefer new technology over traditional methods. But I think some of us are trying to change this trend. If more people realize the value of these skills, they might come back to the workshops.
Yes, I hope so. Let's go to the workshop together next Saturday.
Of course. We can go by the bike-sharing service to save money. Well, I'll bring the tea set we bought yesterday. Let's enjoy the evening together.

messages.content: Hi, I'm Lin Fang. I love hiking here in Guilin. I've been thinking about going to the old stone forests in Xingping Town, but I heard the weather is tricky right now. What do you think?

Well, actually, the spring rain is very common in Guilin this time of year. If you go to the stone forests, you might get your shoes wet, but the mist makes the limestone look magical. I mean, it's beautiful in a different way when it's damp.
That sounds risky, but I really want to see the rocks close up. By the way, does the rain affect the tea picking nearby? I read that farmers stop harvesting working when it rains heavily.

Oh, yes, it does. You know, the tea leaves need dry weather to be picked properly. If it rains for three days straight, the farmers have to wait because the leaves are too wet to harvest. Actually, we usually wait until the sun comes out in the afternoon.
I see. So if I hike now, maybe I can't buy any fresh local tea? That's a shame because I love Chinese tea. What kind do you recommend?

Well, you can still buy some, but the best leaves are usually reserved for drier days. I'd say try the local longjing tea from Xingping. It's very light and goes well with the mountain air. You could also have some hot jasmine tea to warm up if it gets chilly on the trail.
Jasmine tea sounds perfect! But I'm worried about the trails. With so many tourists coming here lately, are the paths to the stone forests still safe and natural?

Actually, it's a bit of a trade-off. On one hand, the trails are very well maintained now, so you won't get lost. On the other hand, so many visitors mean some parts are getting crowded. Honestly, the ancient paths used to be quieter, but now there are more steps and signs because of the tourism.
That makes sense. I guess I have to choose between seeing fewer people or having safer paths. Is there a time of day when it's less busy?

Yes, early morning is the best time. Most tour groups arrive after breakfast, so if you go before nine, you'll have the trails to yourself. Also, the light is better for photos then. It's a small sacrifice, but it's worth it for a quieter experience.
Early morning it is! One more thing, if the weather suddenly turns bad while I'm hiking, what should I do? Do I have a plan?

Of course, you should check the forecast again before you leave. If the weather turns bad, the local guides can help you find shelter or take the bus back down. The stone forest area has a few small pavilions, but it's safer to turn back if the wind is strong.
Thanks for the advice, Neighbor. I feel much better now. I'll head to Xingping Town early tomorrow morning and maybe grab some breakfast at a local snack shop first.
You're welcome, Lin Fang. Just remember, the morning buns and soy milk are the best there. Have a safe hike, and don't forget to bring a raincoat! It's always good to be prepared in Guilin.

messages.content: Hi, I'm Lin Fang. I'm planning to hike up to those old stone forests near Xingping Town today. Do you think the trails are safe now?

Well, the trails are generally safe, but it depends on the weather. Actually, if the morning mist hasn't cleared yet, some parts of the path might be a bit slippery. You know, I've seen many hikers slip when the ground is damp.
That's a good point. How has the weather been lately in Guilin? I heard the rain has been affecting everything.

Yes, it's been quite wet. In fact, the rain last week delayed the tea picking season in our village. Since the leaves were too young, the farmers couldn't harvest the Longjing tea yet. They had to wait for the sun to dry them properly.
Wow, I didn't know that. So the quality of the tea changes depending on the rain, right? What if there is too much moisture?

Exactly. If there is too much moisture, the leaves can go bad quickly. The farmers have to cover the tea bushes with bamboo mats to let the air circulate. By the way, this year the harvest might be smaller because of the persistent clouds.
I see. I'm worried that too many tourists are coming to these places. Do you think the crowds are damaging the natural trails?

To be honest, the number of visitors has increased significantly over the past decade. Some sections of the stone forest path have been eroded because of the heavy foot traffic. However, the local government has started limiting the number of hikers allowed on the trail each day.
That sounds like a reasonable solution. But will it really help if people still want to take photos everywhere?

It tends to help, but it's not a complete fix. Many tourists don't realize how much their cameras weigh down the ancient stones. I've noticed that some guides now ask visitors to place their gear on rocks instead of standing directly on them.
That's interesting. Maybe they should teach them more about respecting the nature. What do you think about hiring more local guides?

Hiring more local guides would definitely be beneficial. They know exactly which parts of the trail are fragile and can explain the history of the stone formations. In some sense, education is more important than just restricting the number of people.
You're right. I think I'll hire a guide next time. Is there a specific person you recommend?

Well, my neighbor Uncle Wei is quite experienced. He's been guiding tourists for over twenty years. He can tell you stories about the legends of the stone forests that you won't find in any guidebook. He's very patient with foreigners.
Great! I'll ask for Uncle Wei's contact information. Thank you for all the advice, I feel much more prepared now.

messages.content: Hello. I'm Zhao Lei. I'm leading a new volunteer program here in our neighborhood near Tianfu Square. Actually, I think we could organize a small festival this weekend if people are interested.

Well, that's a wonderful idea, Zhao Lei. You know, our neighborhood used to have a similar event back when I was working here, but things have changed. Honestly, I think many people are busy now, but if we make it fun, they will come.
I agree. We could invite the kids to make some traditional paper cuttings. By the way, have you ever tried the dumpling making competition we could hold? It tends to be a big hit in Chengdu.

Oh, dumplings! Yes, of course. My wife used to make the best ones in the whole district, you know. If we have a competition, I'd love to be a judge. Actually, I remember eating spicy hot pot last year, and it was delicious. Maybe we can serve that too?

That sounds great. But organizing a festival takes time. I've been thinking about how community centers in our city help connect neighbors. If we have a central place, it might be easier to manage everything.

You're right. The community center across the street has been quiet for years, but perhaps we could use it this time. I think the local government would support us, actually. It's not just about food, you see. It's about building relationships that last.

I see your point. In some sense, modern life makes us feel lonely even when we live close to each other. Well, what if we asked the elderly residents to share stories instead of just cooking? They have so much experience.

That's a brilliant idea. Many of them miss sharing their lives with the younger generation. In fact, I remember my neighbor Mr. Liu telling me stories about the old train station. If we create a storytelling corner, it could be very meaningful.

Exactly. And we can invite students from nearby universities to help with the setup. They have energy, and they need practice too. Do you think we could get the transit lines to bring people from further away?

Well, the subway lines are very convenient now, so that shouldn't be a problem. I mean, people love the new Line 2. However, traffic can be bad during rush hour. If we schedule the festival in the evening, it might be better for everyone.
That makes sense. I'll draft a plan with these ideas. By the way, what's your name again? I want to make sure everyone knows who's helping.

Oh, right. I'm Lin Hong. I've lived here since the 1990s, so I know the history well. Honestly, it's been years since I felt so involved in something new. Let's hope this festival brings our community together again.

messages.content: Hi, Mr. Li. It is a hot day, right? I am planning to start a new volunteer project in our neighborhood at Tianfu Square. Do you have any ideas?

Well, yes, it is quite hot in Chengdu during summer. I think a community center event would be perfect. Actually, we could organize a traditional festival in the square. You know, many young families live there now, but they rarely use the public spaces.
That sounds interesting. But is it possible to get people to participate? I heard many adults are busy with work.

Honesty, it is a challenge. However, if we focus on something fun, like making Tangyuan or playing traditional games, they might join. In the past, neighbors would gather for festivals, but now everyone is too busy. I mean, the community center has some free space we could use.
I see. If we use the center, maybe the local government will support us with food. What do you think about the costs?

That is a good point. Well, the government tends to support cultural activities, but the money is not enough for a big festival. We could ask local businesses for help. For example, the tea shop on Jinyu Road might donate some snacks. You know, people love free tea and pastries.
Yes, the tea shop is very popular. Maybe they will agree. Also, how can we encourage teenagers to help? They are usually not interested in volunteer work.

Actually, teenagers are different now. They want to share their own culture, not just learn old traditions. If we let them design the festival decorations or teach others about street food, they will be very active. In some sense, they feel more in control when they lead the activity.
That is a great idea. I have not thought about letting them lead. What if we invite elderly people to teach them about dumpling making? It would be a nice way to connect generations.

Of course! My wife used to make the best dumplings in the neighborhood. She would love to teach them. It has been years since we gathered like this. The past was much simpler, but now we can create new memories. I think the kids will learn a lot from the elders.
Yes, learning from elders is important. If we invite them, maybe we should also provide a small reward. Do you think that is necessary?

Well, a reward is not the main point, but it helps. Perhaps we can offer certificates or small gifts like fresh fruit. Actually, I remember when I was young, people did not need money to feel valued. But now, a little recognition makes a big difference. Let us plan the details soon.
I agree. Thank you for your advice, Mr. Li. I will start talking to the tea shop owner. Maybe we can meet again next week to discuss the schedule.

That sounds like a good plan. By the way, please make sure to check the weather forecast. If it rains, we might need to move the activity to the center hall. Anyway, I am looking forward to seeing your project succeed. It is good for the whole neighborhood.

messages.content: Hi, I'm Huang Xin. I'm looking for a good place to eat hand-pulled noodles today, but I don't want to go to the big chains.

Well, you're in the right place. I own this small shop in North Gate Market, and we make authentic Lanzhou beef noodles here every day. It's not a chain, so the taste is different from what you'd find in a big mall.
That sounds perfect. I've heard that the broth is the most important part, but I'm not sure how it's made without a machine.

Actually, we use a special bone broth that's been simmering for over twelve hours. My father started this recipe thirty years ago, and we still follow it exactly. It takes time, but it gives the soup a rich flavor that machines can't copy.
Wow, that's impressive. Do you think people still buy this kind of food, or is everyone eating at fast food restaurants now?

You know, that's a good question. Honestly, younger people are changing their habits. Some of them prefer quick meals because they're in a rush. But many locals still come here, especially in the morning, because they value the taste more than speed.
I see. What about the noodles themselves? Are they different from what I had in Chengdu?

I mean, they are similar in being hand-pulled, but the texture is unique. In Lanzhou, we pull them until they are thick and chewy, while in other places they might be thinner. Also, the beef chunks we use is fresh and sliced very thin, which makes a big difference.
Okay, I think I'll try the 'Da' style. Is that the one with the extra oil on top?

Yes, that's correct. The 'youmian' has a generous amount of chili oil and vinegar that makes the soup spicy and aromatic. Well, it might be too hot for you if you're not used to it, but it's delicious if you like it.
I like spicy food, so that's fine. But I'm wondering if the menu changes depending on the time of day. Like, is lunch different from breakfast?

To be honest, the main dish is the same, but the serving times matter. Most people eat this for breakfast or lunch, around noon. In the evening, fewer people come because it's a heavy meal, but we still serve it if you want.
That makes sense. Since it's winter outside, I guess people prefer something warm like this rather than cold drinks.

Exactly! It's cold outside, so the hot soup is perfect. Many customers come just to keep warm. By the way, do you drink tea with your meal? We have a special local tea that pairs well with the noodles.

messages.content: Hi, I'm Huang Xin. It's really cold here today in Lanzhou. I want to find a good place for lunch. Do you know any real local noodle shops near this market?

Well, if you're looking for authentic food, you should try the shop behind the vegetable stalls. It's called Ma's Hand-Pulled Noodles, and it has been open for over thirty years. I've been coming there since I was a child, so I think it's one of the best spots in the area.
That sounds interesting. What kind of noodles do they serve? I usually eat beef noodles in Chengdu, but I've never tried Lanzhou beef noodles before. Is it different?

Actually, yes, it is quite different. In Lanzhou, the broth is usually clearer and has a stronger aroma from the spices, like cumin and chili oil. The noodles are pulled by hand, which makes them very chewy. Also, we often eat them for breakfast, but many people have dinner here too, especially in winter when it's cold.
I see. So the difference between morning and evening meals is just the temperature of the broth? Or is there something else?

To be honest, it's more about the timing and the ingredients. In the morning, people often add lamb or beef to warm up quickly. But in the evening, some shops serve slightly richer broths with extra vegetables. However, the quality of the noodles doesn't change. They are always fresh.

That makes sense. But I'm a bit worried. My friends in Shanghai told me that younger people in China don't like traditional food anymore. They prefer fast food or Western chains. Do you think this shop will still be popular?

Well, I think your friends might be exaggerating. Sure, many young people eat at KFC or McDonald's sometimes, but they still love traditional flavors. In fact, I see a lot of university students from Gansu University coming here every day. They know that homemade food tastes better than anything in a factory.
Really? Even though they have so many choices? Maybe they miss the taste of home. Should I order the spicy beef noodle soup then?

Yes, definitely. The spicy beef noodle soup is famous here, and the chili oil is made fresh every morning. It's not too spicy for most people, but it adds a nice kick to the meal. By the way, don't forget to add some garlic water if you like, although some people find it too strong.
Gar garlic water? I didn't know about that. Is it common in other cities too, or just in Lanzhou?

It's mostly a Lanzhou tradition. People believe that garlic water helps digest the heavy meat and spices. In other cities, like Xi'an, they might serve vinegar instead. But here, we stick to our own methods because they work well for us.
I understand now. Tradition tradition is important. I think I will try this place. How much will a bowl cost? I don't want to spend too much money.

Don't worry, the prices are very reasonable. A bowl of beef noodle soup costs about ten to fifteen yuan. You can even get a side dish of pickled radish for free sometimes. It's a great value for the quality you get. You should try it while the soup is still hot.
Thank you very much for your advice. I'll go there right away. I hope the weather gets better soon so I can eat outside more often.
Of course, I'm happy to help. And yes, the winter in Lanzhou is tough, but once you eat a hot bowl of noodles, you'll feel much better. Enjoy your lunch!

messages.content: Grandma, I just downloaded a new video app on my phone, but I can't find the red heart button. Where did you put it?

Well, actually, that red heart isn't for liking videos anymore, you know. It used to be there, but now the interface is different because they added so many new features. You might have accidentally deleted the icon, or maybe you're looking at the wrong screen.
Oh, I see. I tried to call Dad, but his number shows as 'Busy' or something. Is he busy or is there a problem?

That's strange. Usually, if he's busy, it says 'busy', but 'i' usually means the call was failed because the signal was weak. Oh, by the way, did you check if his phone is on silent mode? Sometimes older phones get stuck like that.
Maybe. But I also saw a message saying he went to a park near the Bell Tower. Do you think he's walking with Uncle Lin again?

Well, that makes sense. They tend to walk there every afternoon, especially when the weather is like this cool autumn air. It's a good place for them to talk, and it's not too far from where I live, so I'm not worried about their safety.
I wish I could join them. But I have to study for my exam at Xi'an Jiaotong University tomorrow. It's really stressful.

I understand, studying is hard work, and exams are important. But you know, you don't have to do everything alone. If you feel too tired, maybe you could call them on the phone instead of meeting them in person. That way, you can rest a bit.
That's a good idea. But sometimes I feel guilty because I'm not helping them as much as Mom does. She cooks them hotpot every weekend.

Actually, Mom does most of the cooking because she knows exactly how they like their food, like the spicy mutton hotpot. But you can help in other ways, like teaching them how to use WeChat Pay or sending them funny videos. That's also a kind of care, right?
Yes, you are right. I should try to teach them how to scan the QR code at the supermarket. It's hard for them, but they want to try.

Well, that's very kind of you. They've been used to giving money in cash for a long time, so changing that habit is not easy. But if you take your time and be patient, they will learn eventually. It's a process, you know.
I'll try to be patient. Maybe after I finish my exam, we can go to the supermarket together and I'll show them step by step.

That sounds like a great plan. And don't forget, after you study, you should come back and have some noodles with us. The beef noodles at the old shop near the gate are still the best, even after all these years.
Okay, I promise. I'll eat the noodles and then help them with the QR code. Thanks for understanding my exam stress, Grandma.
Of course, I understand. Family is important, and you're doing your best. Just take care of your studies and don't worry too much about the rest. We'll be here waiting for you.

messages.content: Grandma, I just bought a new phone for you yesterday. It's very light, but I'm afraid you won't understand how to use it.
Well, thank you, Jie. You've always been so considerate of us old people. Actually, I'm quite interested in learning, but the interface seems so confusing. How did it work before?
My old phone was clunky and had small buttons. This one is different because everything is on a screen. If you tap the right icon, you can video call me instantly.
I see. So, it's like talking through a picture? But honestly, the battery drains so quickly. In our village, we used to save every drop of water. Do we really need to charge this every day?
I know it sounds wasteful, but modern life is fast. If you don't charge it, the power goes off. Maybe we can talk later? I'm going to help you download some photos of your garden first.
Oh, that's a good idea. By the way, I took pictures of the peonies blooming in the courtyard. They were beautiful last week, even though the autumn wind was blowing hard.
That reminds me. We should go to the Bell Tower tomorrow morning. It tends to be crowded, but the air is fresh. You can show me those photos on my phone while we walk there.
Really? I haven't been there since I was young. The noise of the city has changed so much. I suppose if I can learn this, I might feel less left behind by the younger generation.
Don't worry about it. We all adapt at different speeds. Some people struggle with the technology, but they eventually get used to it. Have you ever tried ordering food on the app?
Not yet. I usually go to the market to buy fresh noodles and dumplings. It's more reliable, don't you think? Sometimes the delivery takes too long for my taste.
That's true, the food from the market is always better. But if you order online, you can get hot soup delivered to our door. It's convenient when it's raining and we can't go out.
Well, I see your point. Maybe I will try it once. After all, life is about making choices between tradition and convenience. What do you say, grandson?

messages.content: Hi Zhang, I am really thinking about quitting my job at the design firm in Nanshan. The overtime is so bad, I almost never see my family on weekends.

Well, I completely understand your worry. You know, the pressure in Shenzhen can be overwhelming, especially for creatives. If you leave now, you might lose some stability, but staying like this will probably affect your mental health in the long run.
That is true. I have been working until midnight for weeks. My boss said if I do not finish the project by Friday, I will not get promoted. But I feel exhausted.

Honestly, that sounds like a tough spot. It tends to be the case that companies in China value output over balance right now. However, if you keep going at this pace, you might burn out before you even get the promotion you want.
Maybe. But I am worried about the money. Starting a studio in Futian would cost a lot, and I have a mortgage on my apartment in Bao'an.

By the way, the cost of setting up a studio is high, and you are right about the mortgage pressure. If you start a business now, you might face financial stress for a while. But, you could consider a smaller project first to test the market without taking too much risk.
I have an idea. I want to take some weekend classes to learn photography. It could be a side project. What do you think of this?

That sounds like a great idea. Actually, developing a side interest while working full-time can be a smart move. It gives you a chance to build a portfolio and maybe find new clients without quitting your job immediately.
Yes, I will try that. But my friend told me the competition in the design industry is very fierce. Many young people are doing it too.

You know, competition is fierce everywhere, but having a unique style can help you stand out. If you focus on something specific, like urban landscapes or portraits local culture, you might find your own niche.
I am not sure if I can do it alone. Sometimes I feel like I am stuck in a cycle of hard work and no reward.

I think it is normal to feel stuck sometimes. Many people go through a phase where the rewards do not match the effort. Perhaps you should talk to a few other designers in Nanshan to see how they handle similar situations.
Okay, I will talk to them. Thank you for your advice, Zhang. I will think about starting the photography project next month.
Of course, take your time. Remember, changing careers is a big step, so you should not rush into it. Enjoy your coffee here for a moment and breathe before making any final decisions.

messages.content: Hey, I'm really stressed about my job. The overtime here in Nanshan is crazy. I've been working past 10 PM every day for three months.

Well, that sounds exhausting. You know, many people in Shenzhen feel the same pressure, but honestly, it doesn't have to be this way forever. If you keep this up, your health might suffer more than your career benefits.
I think I want to quit and start my own studio. My friend Li said I should do it, but I'm scared of the risks.

I understand why you're hesitant. Actually, starting a business is risky, especially when you don't have a stable income yet. However, if you wait too long, you might lose your creative energy to the daily grind.
Yes, I've been thinking about it. I saw a designer from Foshan who left his big firm and now he's quite famous online. Maybe I can do that too.

That's a good example. By the way, his story is inspiring, but every situation is different. He probably worked really hard for years before he got famous. You shouldn't expect instant success if you leave your current job.
But I hate the company culture. People always argue over small things. I feel like my ideas are not valued anymore.

Oh, that's really tough. When your ideas are ignored, it can make you feel undervalued. If you stay in such an environment for too long, you might stop believing being creative. It's important to find a place where your work is respected.
Maybe I can keep my job for now and start a small project on weekends? I don't want to lose my savings too quickly.
That sounds like a very wise plan. You could test the waters without risking everything. In some sense, having a side project helps you gain confidence while keeping your safety net intact.
Right. Also, the rent in Nanshan is very high. If I fail, I won't have enough money to live comfortably.

That's a valid concern. The cost of living here is definitely high. You know, many young people move to smaller cities like Zhuhai to save money. Perhaps you could consider that as a backup option if things don't go well.
I think I will try the weekend project first. It gives me time to think clearly without panic.
Exactly. Taking a step back allows you to think clearly. Well, don't forget to take care of your mental health while you decide. Your well-being is more important than any promotion or salary.

messages.content: Hello, I am Hao. It is very hot today in Wuhan. I am confused about the supermarkets near my home in Qingshan District. There are so many places. What do you think?

Well, hello Hao. I am old Li, and I have been working at this wet market for over twenty years. Actually, it is normal to feel confused because there are now big chains like Yonghui and Jiaju competing with us small markets. In some sense, the choice depends on what you need most.
I think the produce quality is very important to me. My children are young. How is the fruit and vegetable quality here compared to the new supermarket down the street?

You know, the quality here is often fresher because we sell straight from the farmers who bring their carts every morning. For example, the bok choy and the dragon fruit at our stall have been picked within hours. However, if you go to a big supermarket, the produce is washed and packaged very neatly, but sometimes it has been sitting for a day or two.
That sounds good. But I am worried about the price. Is the food here cheaper? I have a family budget to manage.

I think the prices vary a lot. Generally, the vegetables here are cheaper per jin, especially if you buy in bulk. But the meat and seafood tend to be more expensive because we have to pay for the ice and the cold storage. So, if you cook at home often, you might save money here, but if you buy ready-to-eat food, the supermarket could be better value.
I see. What about the types of goods? Do I find international brands or special items here that I cannot get at the big store?

By the way, we definitely have items you cannot find anywhere else. You can get fresh river fish like the grass carp, and various local herbs for cooking. We also sell fresh tofu and pickled vegetables that are made right here. The big stores usually only have processed snacks and canned goods, so for traditional Chinese ingredients, we are much better.
That is interesting. Do you offer any customer service or help with cooking? I sometimes do not know how to prepare these local ingredients.

Of course, that is one of our strengths. We often give advice on how to cook the fish or which tofu goes best with a soy sauce. Sometimes, older customers even share family recipes. In a big supermarket, you just buy the product and leave, but here, you can talk to the vendor about your meal plans.
That sounds very nice. Do you have a loyalty program? I like to buy things regularly, so I want to know if I can save more points or get discounts.

We do have a simple card system for regular customers. If you use our membership card, you get a small discount on every purchase, and we sometimes give extra eggs or free tea leaves on your birthday. However, the big supermarkets have those complex apps with points that can be exchanged for movie tickets or gifts, which might appeal to younger people more.
I am thinking about using the app for the points, but I want to support local farmers too. Which option do you recommend for a family like mine?

Honestly, it depends on your priorities. If supporting local agriculture and getting fresher food is more important, then this wet market is the right choice. You can also help the local economy by buying here. But if you want the convenience of online delivery and those digital rewards, the big chains are designed for that lifestyle. There is no perfect answer, really.
Thank you for your advice, Old Li. I think I will try the membership card here first, and then I will compare the prices on my next shopping trip. It is helpful to know.

That is a great plan, Hao. You are very wise to compare both options. Please remember that the market closes early in the summer heat, so come before the sun sets. We hope to see you soon, and if you need any help weighing the fish, just call out!

messages.content: Hey, I'm Hao. I live in the Qingshan District now. Honestly, I'm totally confused by all the different grocery stores. Some are huge supermarkets, and others are just small wet markets. What's the difference?

Well, Hao, it's a common question for new residents. Actually, the wet markets here in Qingshan tend to be much more traditional. You know, you can see the fish being cleaned right there, and the vegetables are often picked from farms in Hubei just yesterday. In the big supermarkets, though, everything is packaged, so it's very convenient, but maybe not as fresh.
That makes sense. But I'm worried about the price. Do you think the wet markets are cheaper? I'm trying to save money for my daughter's new school bag.

Of course, price is a big factor. I'd say the wet markets are usually cheaper for fresh produce like local greens and seasonal fish. For example, if you buy a kilo of water spinach or some carp, you might pay half the price compared to a chain store like RT-Mart Mart Mart. However, the big supermarkets often have sales on packaged goods and imported items, which can be a better deal if you shop there regularly.
Okay, but what about the quality? My wife says the lettuce at the supermarket is cleaner. Does she have a point?

Hmm, she has a point in some sense. The supermarkets definitely have stricter hygiene standards. They wash the fruits and vegetables before putting them in the plastic bags. But, you know, the wet market vendors usually pick the very best looking items for the display. If you ask nicely, they might even cut the fish for you, which you can't do in a supermarket.
That sounds nice. Do they offer any special services? I don't want to carry heavy bags home alone.

Actually, many wet market vendors are quite helpful. If you ask, they might even deliver the heavy stuff to your doorstep for a small fee. I remember when I moved here, the owner of a small stall near my old apartment used to help me carry things. The supermarkets, on the other hand, have delivery apps now, so that's a plus for them too.
That's really helpful. I haven't thought about delivery before. What about loyalty programs? Do they offer discounts?

Well, the big supermarkets definitely have loyalty cards. You scan the code, and you get points for every yuan you spend. After a certain amount, you can get a discount on next time. The wet markets don't usually have formal cards, but the owners know their regular customers. They might give you a free egg or an extra orange if they see you often, which is a kind of informal loyalty program.
I see. So it depends on what I need. If I just need a few fresh items, the wet market is better. But for household supplies, the supermarket works.

Exactly, you've got the right idea. It tends to be about trade-offs. If you want the freshest seasonal stuff like lotus roots or river shrimp, go to the wet market. But if you need toilet paper or detergent milk, the supermarket is faster and has better brands. Why not try both this week and see which one fits your budget better?
Good idea. Thanks for the advice, vendor. I think I'll start with the wet market for the vegetables.
You're welcome, Hao. Don't worry, the prices are reasonable if you buy in bulk. Just remember to bring a small bag, or I can lend you one. Have a nice evening shopping!

messages.content: Hi, I'm Xia. I'm sitting here in this waiting room in Chang'an District, feeling really tired. My lower back has been hurting for six months now, and it makes it hard for me to teach my students at school.

Oh, I'm so sorry to hear that, Xia. Well, I had something very similar last year. My name is Wei, and I teach Chinese literature in the same district. Actually, the pain started when I was grading papers late into the night, so I understand exactly how frustrating it can be.
That sounds familiar. I've been trying to rest, but I don't think resting is enough. What kind of treatment did you get? Did you go to a big hospital in Beijing or just stay here?

I didn't go to Beijing. In fact, I think local clinics can be just as effective. By the way, I started with acupuncture at a small place near the subway station on the Line 2. It wasn't expensive, and honestly, I felt some relief after the first three sessions.
Acupuncture? I've heard of it, but I'm not sure if it works for back pain. Maybe I should try some medicine or see a specialist who uses Western medicine. What do you think?

Well, I think it depends on your preference. I've seen people who really trust Western medicine and get quick relief from painkillers. However, in my experience, acupuncture tends to work better in the long run. Of course, it's not a magic cure, but it helps reduce the inflammation naturally.
That makes sense. But I'm worried about the cost. My insurance doesn't cover all the alternative therapies. If I have to pay out of pocket, it might be too much money for just trying something new.

I totally get that. The cost of living in Xi'an is rising, and medical bills can add up quickly. Actually, I found a community center in the neighborhood that offered discounted sessions for teachers. You know, it wasn't free, but it was much cheaper than a private clinic.

That's a great idea. I didn't know about community centers. Besides the treatment, do you think I should change my lifestyle? Maybe I should stop carrying my heavy school bag or stop drinking too much tea?

Absolutely. Lifestyle mean, lifestyle changes are crucial if you want to manage the pain. For instance, try to stretch before you start your day, and maybe avoid sitting for too long without standing up. Also, drinking less tea isn't necessary, but staying warm with a hot towel or a cup of ginger tea might help your muscles relax.
I'll try to stretch more. What about my job? Should I ask my principal for some adjustments? I feel like I can't work properly if my back hurts every day.

You should definitely consider asking for adjustments. If you tell your principal what you're going through, they might let you take shorter breaks or help you with some grading tasks. In some sense, being honest about your health is important, and many schools are supportive now.
I hope they are. It feels like I'm stuck between the pain and my work. Maybe I should wait until next week to talk to them. Right now, I just want to get some relief from this waiting room.

Don't worry too much about it right now. Focus on getting that relief first. You could try a simple exercise like the cat-cow stretch if you're feeling brave. I think you'll find that taking care of yourself will make you a better teacher in the long run.

messages.content: Hi Lin. I'm sitting here in this waiting room and my lower back hurts so much. I've been a teacher at a school in Xi'an for five years, but since last autumn, the pain has gotten worse every day.

Oh no, I'm so sorry to hear that. Well, I actually went through something very similar two years ago when I was teaching math in the suburbs. You know, it started with just a dull ache after standing for too long, and then it turned into sharp pain.
That sounds terrible. What did you do? I'm thinking about going to the hospital, but I'm not sure if the treatment is effective here in Chang'an District.

Honestly, the hospitals here are quite good. I went to a clinic near the metro station and saw a specialist who uses traditional Chinese medicine along with modern techniques. It's not a complete cure, but it really helps manage the pain.
Traditional medicine? Do you mean herbal remedies? I'm worried about the side effects. Maybe I should just take painkillers, but I don't want to depend on medicine all the time.

You know, that's a very valid concern. Actually, many people start with herbal teas or moxibustion before trying strong drugs. The key is to find a doctor who explains everything clearly so you feel safe. By the way, did you check if your school has any adjustments for teachers with health issues?

We have a unionwork adjustment policy, but it's very hard to get approved. The principal says we need to be able to stand during the morning assembly. I feel stuck because I can't teach if I'm in so much pain.

That's really tough. Well, in my case, I negotiated a schedule where I could sit down for the first hour of class and then stand only for the second part. It wasn't easy to explain to the administration, but once they saw that I could still do the job safely, they agreed.
I think I might try that. But what about insurance? Will the hospital cover the traditional therapy sessions, or do I have to pay out of my own pocket?

Good question. Usually, the basic insurance covers a lot of standard treatments, but some specialized therapies might be partially covered. You might need to check with your unit's HR department first to see if there are any specific programs for staff health.
I'll ask about that tomorrow. In the meantime, what about lifestyle changes? I eat a lot of noodles and fried food because it's quick, but maybe that's making my back worse.

It tends to be the diet that makes a big difference. I started eating more steamed buns and fresh vegetables instead of heavy oil. It's not a drastic change, but it reduces the inflammation. Also, try to avoid sitting on a hard bench for too long.
That makes sense. I should probably get up and stretch more. Is there a specific exercise you recommend for teachers who stand all day?

Yes, actually, there's a simple routine called 'fiveqigong' that many teachers practice. It involves slow movements and breathing to strengthen the lower back without straining it. You don't need any equipment, just a little space in your home or even outside.

messages.content: Hi Mr. Liu. I want to renovate my old apartment in Huashi District, but I worry about the budget. What do you suggest?

Well, Qiang, it's a good time to think about this. Actually, many people in Dalian are doing the same thing. If you don't set a clear limit first, the costs can add up quickly. You know, the price of materials has gone up recently.
I think the brickwork is the most important part. The walls are old red bricks. Should I paint them or leave them?

That's a classic dilemma. Honestly, painting them completely might hide the history, but leaving them exposed can look dusty. If you choose to restore them, it's a bit more expensive. However, you can mix it: paint the upper part and keep the lower part original. That way, it looks modern but keeps the soul of the building.
I see. What about the windows? They are very small and hard to open. Do I need to change them?

Well, the small windows are typical for old houses in this district. If you replace them with big aluminum ones, the light will be much better, but it might ruin the look of the facade. Actually, you could install some smart glass that is easier to open but keeps the original frame. It's not perfect, but it's a good middle ground.
Oh, I didn't know about smart glass. What about the walls? They are cold in winter. Is insulating them worth the money?

You are absolutely right. The temperature difference in late autumn is quite sharp. If you don't insulate the walls, the heating bill will be very high next winter. It tends to be a wise investment, even if it costs a lot upfront. You could use some thin thermal paper that doesn't change the thickness of the wall too much.
That sounds expensive. How do I find a contractor who is not too costly? Many people say there are too many bad workers.

I think you should ask around in the courtyard first. You know, Mr. Zhang next door recommended a team last year. They were honest and didn't ask for extra money later. If you ask for references from their past projects, you can see if the work quality is good. Don't just hire the first person who offers the lowest price.
That is a good idea. But what if I want to add some modern furniture? Will the old layout be a problem?

Well, the layout might be a bit tight. Actually, many old apartments in Dalian have small rooms that are hard to fit modern sofas in. You can try moving the furniture to the hallway or use smaller pieces. If you remove a wall to make a bigger space, it needs to be done by a professional. Otherwise, you might break the structure.
I am worried about breaking the structure. Is there a rule for this?

Of course, there are strict rules about structural changes. The government checks the building safety very carefully. If you knock down a load-bearing wall, you will get into big trouble. I would say it's safer to keep the main walls and just change the non-structural parts. That way, you stay safe and within the law.

messages.content: Hello, neighbor. I am thinking about renovating my apartment in the Huashi District, but I am worried about losing the old brick style.

Well, I think you can keep the charm if you are careful. Actually, many people in Dalian do this because the red bricks are very special. You just need to find a contractor who knows how to repair them instead of painting over everything.
That is a good idea. But I read that the old windows were not insulated, so it is very cold in winter.

Of course, it is quite cold in late autumn here. You could replace the glass with double-pane ones, but you should try to keep the original wooden frames if possible. That way, the house still feels historic, but it will be much warmer inside.
I want to insulate the walls too. Is it easy to do without breaking the plaster?

You know, it is actually a bit tricky. If you add thick insulation inside, the rooms might feel smaller. Some people choose to put it on the outside, but that is a big project. Maybe you should check with a few experts first before making a decision.
My budget is limited, so I cannot spend too much money on the exterior work.

I understand completely. In that case, focusing on the windows and maybe just a thin layer of insulation inside might be better. It is not the cheapest option either, but it is cheaper than tearing down the walls. You have to weigh the cost against how much you want to change the look.
Where can I find a good contractor who speaks English well? I am not sure if I should hire one from the city.

Well, actually, there is a community notice board in the courtyard where people often post ads. You can see if any local workers there know about old buildings. Also, asking around the Huashi area usually helps because everyone knows each other here.
That sounds useful. Do you think I should start with the kitchen or the living room first?

Honestly, I think the living room is more important because you spend more time there. However, if the kitchen leaks water, you have to fix that first. It depends on your priority. If you wait too long to fix the leaks, it might damage the floor you just renovated.
I suppose I will look at the notice board this weekend. Thank you for your advice, neighbor.
You are welcome. I mean, it is always good to talk about these things with someone who lives nearby. By the way, if you need help carrying materials, just let me know. I am happy to help out.

messages.content: Hi, I'm planning to go hiking this weekend. I want to find a good route near Chengdu that is not too crowded. Do you know any places?

Well, if you want to avoid the crowds, you should try the Wenshan district. It is quite close to the city, but it feels very wild. Actually, there is a trail that leads up to the misty mountains behind the old villages. You can start from the local bus station, and it takes about twenty minutes to get there.
That sounds nice. But I heard it rains a lot in Chengdu. Will the fog make it hard to see the path?

You know, the fog is actually a huge part of the experience here. In early spring, the mountains tend to be covered in a thick white mist most of the time. It might be hard to see far ahead, but that is exactly what makes it special. If you go on a clear day, it feels too normal. I think the humidity helps the plants grow so fast, even in the shade.
I see. So the weather makes the view different. What kind of plants can we see there?

Honestly, you will see some rare bamboo forests and lots of moss. The trees are very green because the air is so moist. By the way, I remember seeing a small waterfall stream that was full of clear water. It was cold, but it was refreshing after walking up the steep rocks.
That sounds amazing. Are there any other nature spots nearby that we can visit if we have more time?

Of course, there are. You could drive a bit further to the Qionglai foothills. It is a bit far, but the scenery is more dramatic. Some people say that the wildflowers animals like deer are more common there than in Wenshan. However, the roads are not as good, so you need a strong car. I've been to both, and each has its own charm.
I think I will stick to Wenshan for now since it is closer. How do we get the food there?

Well, you cannot buy much food on the trail itself. Most hikers pack their own lunch. If you want something local, you can buy some spicy cold noodles at the village market before you start. They are very popular and perfect for keeping you full. You can also bring some pickled vegetables, which go well with the hot weather.
Spicy noodles sound good. I like Sichuan food. What should I wear for the hike?

Actually, you should wear layers. It is not very cold, but the temperature drops quickly when you go up the mountain and the wind blows. A light jacket is essential, even in spring. Also, bring good shoes because the path can be muddy and slippery. I've seen people fall just because their boots were not waterproof.
Good point. I will pack a jacket and good shoes. Do you think we need a guide or can we go alone?

I'd say you can go alone if you are careful, but a guide is safer for the first time. The signs on the trail are sometimes not very clear in the fog. If you get lost, it can be scary. Many local groups offer half-day tours where a guide leads the way and they stop at interesting spots. It is worth the extra money for peace of mind.
That makes sense. I will look for a guide then. Thanks for your help, Lin.
You're welcome! It is really a great trip. Just remember to take a raincoat in case the weather changes suddenly. Have a wonderful weekend in the mountains!

messages.content: Hey, I'm planning a weekend hiking trip near Chengdu. Do you have any good routes in mind?

Well, actually, I'd say you should check out the area around Wenshan district, since we are talking about your current location. It's got some great trails that lead into the misty mountains without being too far from the city. If you head towards Xindu, you can find some really quiet paths.
That sounds perfect. But I heard the weather this spring is quite unpredictable. How does the mist affect visibility on those trails?

You know, the fog can be quite thick in the morning, so you might not see the peaks clearly. However, it tends to burn off by midday, which makes the view much better. Honestly, it creates this magical atmosphere where the trees look like they are floating, but you have to be careful not to get lost.
I'm worried about getting lost if I can't see the signs. Have you ever used a map app there?

Oh, absolutely. I always use Baidu Maps, and it's much more reliable than Google Maps in rural areas. You should definitely download the offline map before you go, just in case the signal gets weak. By the way, the trail markers are usually well-maintained, so it's not as scary as it sounds.
Okay, I'll do that. What should I pack? Do I need a tent or just a day bag?

Actually, since the weather is so changeable, I'd recommend carrying a small umbrella and a light raincoat. You don't need a tent unless you plan to stay overnight, but a day bag is essential for water and snacks. It's also a good idea to bring some warm clothes, even in spring, because it gets chilly up high.
Got it. Are there any specific food spots nearby where we can stop for a break?

Yes, there are a few small tea houses along the path where people sell local snacks. You can try some roasted chestnuts or sweet potatoes that are common there. They are cheap and delicious, and they help keep you warm during the walk.
That sounds amazing. Is it hard to find these places or are they hard to find?

They are actually quite easy to spot if you look for signs. Many locals gather there in the afternoon to relax after work. It's a nice way to take a break from the trail and enjoy some local culture. I mean, it's a great way to experience the region beyond just hiking.
I love the idea of combining hiking with local culture. Do you think we should combine other nature spots as well?

Definitely. After the hike, you could visit the nearby wetlands or botanical gardens that are famous in Chengdu. It's a good balance between the rugged mountain trails and more peaceful environments. If you go in the evening, you might even see some nocturnal birds, which adds another layer to the experience.
That sounds like a perfect plan. I think I will book my tickets now.
Excellent choice. Just remember to check the bus schedule from the city center, as some routes stop running earlier than you might expect. Have a safe trip, and I hope you enjoy the misty mountains!

messages.content: Hello, I'm Jie. I used to teach English at the local school, but now I'm retired. I feel like I haven't done enough since I stopped working. There's an old community garden in our neighborhood in Yuhua district that looks very neglected. The soil is dry and the paths are cracked. I was wondering if you need volunteers to help restore it. I think it would be great for the children nearby to have a green space.

Well, Jie, that's a wonderful idea, and honestly, we're looking for exactly that kind of experience. Actually, the project manager has been saying that the garden needs someone who understands plants and community dynamics. If you join us, we could start by clearing the overgrown weeds and then replanting some local vegetables like bok choy and tomatoes. By the way, your teaching background might be very useful for organizing the younger kids later on.

That sounds interesting. I remember how hard it is to find a good balance between helping others and enjoying my free time. When I was young, I worked very hard, so now I want to relax a bit. But I know that if I stay in the house all day, I feel useless. The summer weather here in Nanjing is quite hot and humid, which makes me want to stay inside. Do you think working outside in this weather is too much for someone my age?

You know, the weather is indeed tough, but we usually schedule the heavy work for the early mornings or late afternoons to avoid the peak heat. In some sense, staying inside all day can make us feel disconnected from the neighborhood, so stepping out is actually good for your mental health. We also have breaks where everyone sits under the big ginkgo trees and shares cold sweet potato noodles or shaved ice to cool down. It tends to be much more manageable than you might expect.

I see. Speaking of food, the sweet potato noodles sound delicious. But I am a bit worried about the organization. Last year, a festival we planned turned into a mess because people arrived at different times. If I volunteer, will there be a clear schedule? I don't want to cause more problems. Also, I have a small grandson who visits me every weekend, and I need to make sure he gets enough attention.

Actually, we've learned from last year's mistakes, so don't worry. We now have a strict timeline and a group chat where everyone confirms their arrival time before coming. To be honest, the festivals are much smoother now because we assigned specific roles to everyone. Regarding your grandson, we have a flexible policy where volunteers can bring their families to the events. In fact, having kids there often makes the atmosphere much livelier. Would you consider joining a weekend cleanup session first, just to see how it fits with your routine?

That sounds reasonable. I think I would like to try a weekend session. But I must admit, I am not very good at organizing large groups. When I taught, I had a class of thirty students, but managing a group of neighbors feels different. They might ask for things that are not possible. What should I do if I feel overwhelmed? I have heard that volunteers often quit because they feel too much pressure.

Well, that's a very common concern, but you are not alone in feeling that way. Honestly, no one expects a retired teacher to be a perfect manager. The coordinator, Mr. Li, will handle the heavy logistics, and you can focus on guiding the activities. If things get too much, you can always step back or ask for a break. Many volunteers quit not because of the work itself, but because they didn't feel supported. We try to ensure that everyone feels heard, so I'm sure you'll find your place here.

Thank you for reassurance. You know, I have a different perspective on volunteering. I used to think it was only about giving, but now I realize it's also about receiving. If I help the garden, maybe I will receive friendship and a sense of belonging. The neighborhood has changed a lot over the years. Many old families have moved to the suburbs, and the streets feel quieter. I miss the noise and the laughter of the old days.

You're absolutely right, and that's exactly why this project is so meaningful. When the old families moved to the suburbs, the community spirit faded, and that's what we're trying to bring back. Restoring the garden is just the first step; eventually, we plan to hold monthly festivals where neighbors from different streets can meet and share stories. It tends to create a new sense of belonging for both the older residents and the new young families moving in. You might even make some new friends who can share your love for cooking traditional dishes.

That is very encouraging. I would love to cook for the festival. My family makes a special braised pork belly with rice, but I'm not sure if everyone in the neighborhood would like it. Maybe I can prepare some vegetarian dumplings instead, which are more popular. What do you think about the timing? The Mid-Autumn Festival is coming up next month. Should we prepare for that?

Oh, that's a brilliant idea! Well, braised pork belly is a classic, but yes, dumplings are definitely a crowd-pleaser, so maybe we can offer both. As for the timing, Mid-Autumn Festival is a great opportunity, but we might start smaller with a summer harvest celebration in July. If we try something big too soon, we might get overwhelmed, so it's better to build up slowly. That said, if you're ready, we can discuss the details for the summer event next week. What do you think?

I think starting smaller is a good idea. It gives me time to adjust my schedule. I have a lot of hobbies, like reading and listening to classical traditional music, and I don't want to give them up completely. However, if I can see a real difference in the garden, I will be happy to dedicate more time. It's important to find a balance, you know. I feel that if I serve the community, the community will also care for me when I am old and sick.

That is a beautiful perspective, Jie. Honestly, there's a strong reciprocal of reciprocity in our community, and people really do look out for one another. We've seen neighbors helping each other carry heavy boxes or sharing umbrellas in the rain, and that sense of care is exactly what we hope to strengthen. So, let's start with the weekend garden cleanup next Saturday. We'll meet at the main gate around eight in the morning. messages.content: Hi, I'm Jie. I'm a retired teacher and I want to help restore the old community garden in our Yuhua neighborhood. It used to be very nice, but now it's full of weeds.

Well, that's wonderful, Jie! I think your experience would be really valuable. Actually, we've been looking for someone with your background to guide the volunteers. By the way, have you checked the soil conditions recently?
I haven't checked the soil yet. I'm worried it might be too hard to fix. Also, I'm not sure if I have enough time because my grandchildren visit me from the university nearby.

You know, I completely understand your concern about your family time. In fact, most of our volunteers balance their work with their family duties. If you join the planning committee, we can schedule tasks on weekends when the kids are usually at school or with relatives. That way, you can still spend time with them.
That sounds reasonable. But organizing festivals is also on the list. I heard there will be a Mid-Autumn Festival celebration soon. Do you think I should help with that too?

Honestly, I think combining the garden project with the festival could work well. You see, if we plant some chrysanthemums and osmanthus now, they will bloom right around the Mid-Autumn Festival. That would make the celebration much more meaningful for everyone in the neighborhood.
Oh, that's a great idea! I remember my mother used to make mooncakes with lotus seed paste. Maybe I could teach the younger volunteers how to make them.

That would be amazing! The younger generation really misses these traditions. Well, I've noticed that many young people are eager to learn about local customs. If you share your recipes, it might help preserve our culture in a practical way.
Yes, I agree. But sometimes I feel tired after teaching at the school for many years. Do you think volunteering is too much for someone my age?

I think you're overestimating the workload. Actually, we have a small team that handles the heavy lifting. Your role would be more about supervision giving advice and encouraging people. In some sense, it's more rewarding than physically demanding, and it helps keep you active too.
That makes me feel better. I just don't want to let down the neighbors who invited me. What if something goes wrong during the festival?

Don't worry, we've faced similar situations before. If there are any problems, the whole team will step in to solve them. You don't have to carry the burden alone. As long as you show up and share your ideas, we'll manage the rest.
Alright, I'll join the committee. But I need to know the exact schedule so I can tell my grandchildren. They love visiting the old teahouse near the park.

Of course! I'll send you the detailed schedule by tomorrow. We usually meet at the community center near the old teahouse, so you can visit them before or after your meetings. That way, everyone is happy.

messages.content: Hi Lin. It's really cold here in Liwan today. I'm trying to make my grandmother's wontons, but the dough keeps cracking.

Well, I think the humidity might be the issue. You know, Guangzhou is usually quite damp, even in winter, so the dough doesn't need to rest as long as it does in the north. Have you tried letting it sit for an hour before rolling it out?
Actually, I did let it rest, but maybe not long enough. My mom always said you have to cover it with a damp cloth. I used a regular one.
That's probably it. If the cloth is too dry, the surface of the dough will dry out and crack. By the way, are you using pork and chive filling, or something different?
Yes, pork and chive. It tastes better than the chicken one my aunt makes in Chengdu. But my filling tastes a bit salty.
I see. Well, maybe you added too much soy sauce. In my family, we tend to add the salt to the pork itself, not the sauce, so it doesn't get too salty. Also, did you mix the oil in before the water?
No, I added the water first. My grandma said that makes the layers stick together. But now I'm worried I messed up the recipe.

Don't worry too much. Actually, recipes vary a lot depending on the region. In northern places like Beijing, they might use different techniques, but in the south, we often add water first. You'll get the hang of it with practice.
I hope so. Do you like cooking with your family? My parents used to cook together, but now they just order food.

Honestly, I miss those days. We used to make baozi and youtiao every Sunday. It's not just about the food, but the time we spend together. Now that I live here, I try to invite my neighbors over to cook too.
That sounds nice. Maybe I should invite you next time. We could make dumplings together and share them.
That would be wonderful. You know, group cooking is much more fun than cooking alone. We can chat while we chop vegetables and knead the dough. It really helps the time pass faster.
Yes, talking makes the work feel easier. I'll try the damp cloth trick tomorrow. Thanks for your help.
Of course. Just remember to cover the dough well. Also, if the dough is too stiff, add a little warm water. Good luck with your wontons.

messages.content: Hi Aunt Mei, I'm trying to organize a Mid-Autumn reunion dinner for all our cousins. We haven't seen each other in years since I moved to Chongqing, and the others are scattered across the country.

Well, that's a wonderful idea, especially during the Mid-Autumn Festival. Actually, family gatherings like this are becoming less common now, so it's quite special. Do you have a specific place in mind, or are you still deciding where to hold it?

I was thinking of going to the Wanda district here. It's busy, and there's a lot of street food around. But I don't want just any restaurant. I want somewhere with some cultural meaning for our family history.

That sounds very thoughtful. You know, the old part of the Wanda area used to be a big trading hub for our clan's ancestors. If you go near the old river bridge, there's a traditional courtyard restaurant there. It tends to have a very nostalgic atmosphere.
Really? That would be perfect. We could share stories about our grandparents while eating. What kind of food would you recommend? I heard the hotpot is famous here.

Yes, the hotpot is definitely iconic, but for a family reunion, maybe a mixed meal is better. You could start with some fresh mooncakes, which are essential this time of year. Then, you can have a hotpot with the spicy broth, followed by some sweet Osmanthus soup at the end.
I like the idea of mixing sweet and savory. My cousin from Shandong might miss the northern style food, though. Should we order some steamed buns with meat from him?

Oh, that's a great point. You know, regional differences are huge in China, and food plays a big part in that. If he brings his own steamed buns, we can make it a fusion dinner. It shows that we respect everyone's background and traditions.
Exactly. I'm worried the younger cousins might find the traditional setting too old-fashioned. They usually prefer modern chains like Starbucks.

I think that's a valid concern, but actually, they might appreciate the change. In some sense, modern people often crave authenticity more than they realize. Plus, if you tell them stories about the old days, they might feel connected to their roots in a new way.
That makes sense. So, if we book the courtyard place near the river, everyone can eat together and talk. It feels more intimate than a big banquet hall.

Absolutely. An intimate setting allows for deeper conversations. You could even ask some elders to share old photos or stories from before they left their hometowns. It will create a nice balance of past and present.
I'll call the restaurant tomorrow and reserve a table for ten. Thanks, Aunt Mei. You always know how to make family events meaningful.

You're welcome, Hao. It's my pleasure to help. Just remember to confirm the reservation later, as places like this get busy quickly during the festival. Let's hope the weather stays clear so everyone can enjoy the full moon!

messages.content: Hi Aunt Lin. I'm organizing a reunion dinner for my cousins this Mid-Autumn Festival. It's been years since we all met. What do you think we should do?

Well, that's a wonderful idea, Hao. You know, family gatherings are very important in our culture. Honestly, I think we should find a place with some historical significance, like an old teahouse in the Jiefangbei district. It would remind everyone of our roots.

That sounds nice, but Jiefangbei might be too crowded. Maybe we could go to a quieter spot near the Yangtze River? Like the old streets in Yubei. My cousin from Guangzhou loves spicy food, so we need a restaurant that serves authentic Chongqing hotpot.

Actually, Yubei is a great choice because the riverside views are beautiful, especially at night. However, I remember that many traditional hotpot shops there have changed since I was a child. If we want the real taste, we might need to go to a smaller alleyway in Nanbin. Also, don't forget to invite Uncle Ming from Shanghai; he hasn't visited in over ten years.

Oh right, I almost forgot Uncle Ming. He lives in a small town in Jiangsu now. By the way, my cousin from Hebei is worried about the travel costs. Do you think we can order some mooncakes online and eat them at home first? That would save money.

I see your point about saving money, but you know, sharing a meal together is much more meaningful than eating separately. If we order food online, it loses the atmosphere of being together. In fact, many elders feel sad if the festival is celebrated without a proper dinner. We could split the bill so that everyone doesn't feel the financial pressure.

messages.content: Hi, I'm Wei. I'm a marketing manager here in Wenzhou. Honestly, I'm thinking about switching jobs. The work pressure here is a bit much, and I don't have the same opportunities as in big cities like Shanghai. What do you think?

Well, that's a tough decision. I've actually worked in Shanghai, so I know the pace is fast. But you know, Wenzhou has its own charm. If you move to Shanghai, the cost of living will go up a lot. In some sense, you might feel more stuck with the traffic and the noise.

That's true. I remember last month I was stuck in the subway for forty minutes. But maybe if I stay, I can save money. However, I feel like my career isn't growing fast enough here. Is remote work an option in smaller towns?

Oh, absolutely. I've seen more companies offering remote setups in the last two years. Many firms based in Hangzhou or Shenzhen hire people from places like Fuzhou or Wenzhou. You don't have to live in the city center to do the job. Actually, it could give you more time for family or hobbies.
That sounds interesting. But will my salary be the same? I'm worried about the difference in income. Also, do you think people in the Old Town district like me are open to these new ideas?

To be honest, the salary might be slightly lower if the company is small, but sometimes the trade-off is worth it. You see, many older colleagues in the Old Town are used to the traditional way, but the younger generation is changing. They want flexibility. It's not just about money anymore.

I see. Maybe I should look into that. What about work-life balance? In my current job, I often work until nine at night. If I switch, can I really change that? I'd say I want more time for my parents in the countryside.

Well, that's a very important point. In the big cities, everyone is always rushing, but in smaller towns, the rhythm is slower. If you find a good role, you might not need to stay late every day. You could even take a walk in the old streets after work instead of staying in the office.

That sounds nice. But I'm not sure if I can handle the change. My last promotion was three years ago. Should I be worried that my skills are becoming outdated? Maybe I need to learn something new first.

I completely understand that feeling. Skills do change, but you've already managed a marketing team, so you have a strong foundation. Actually, many companies value experience over age these days. You could start by taking an online course on digital marketing while looking for a new role.
Okay, that gives me an idea. By the way, do you know any good places to eat near here? I want to try something different from the usual noodles. Maybe something from a local restaurant?

Of course! There's a great restaurant near the Wenzhou Museum that serves authentic local dishes. You should try the grilled river fish; it's delicious. Also, the tea culture here is famous, so you could stop by a teahouse for a break. It's a nice way to relax after a long day.
Thank you! I think I'll go there tomorrow. It's raining outside, so it's perfect for staying inside. I feel more hopeful now about making a move. Maybe the weather in Wenzhou isn't so bad after all.

messages.content: Hi Mr. Zhang, I'm thinking about switching jobs soon. My current role as a marketing manager here in Wenzhou is getting a bit boring, and the salary hasn't gone up much. I feel like I should try to get promoted or find a better opportunity somewhere else.

Well, that's a common feeling, you know. Actually, many of my friends in the marketing industry are looking for better options right now. If you move to a bigger city like Hangzhou, the salaries might be higher, but the cost of living there is also much higher. Have you considered staying in Wenzhou but looking for a different company?

That sounds reasonable, but I'm worried about the career growth. In my old job, I've been doing the same tasks for years. I want to learn new digital marketing skills, like SEO video editing and live streaming, which are very popular now. Do you think there are good training courses in Wenzhou?

I think there are definitely some good options in Wenzhou. There's a vocational college nearby that offers courses in digital media. Of course, the quality might not be as high as in Shanghai, but it's a good start. By the way, many companies in Wenzhou are starting to use live streaming for their products, so it's a great skill to have.

Oh, that's interesting. I didn't know that about live streaming. But honestly, I'm also concerned about work-life balance. In my current office, we often work until late at night. Is it common in big cities too, or is the situation better there?

Actually, the situation is mixed. In big cities like Beijing, the pressure can be even higher because everyone is competing for limited opportunities. However, I've heard that some companies in smaller cities are trying to improve work-life balance to attract talent. You know, having a better life outside of work is becoming more important for many people these days.

That makes sense. I'd prefer a job where I can spend more time with my family. We have a young child, and I want to be there for her. Maybe I should look for a position in a tier-two city where the pace isn't so fast. What do you suggest I do next?

Well, that's a very valid reason. In some sense, raising a child requires a lot of presence from parents. You could look into companies in cities like Ningbo or Shaoxing. They are not as crowded as Shanghai, but they still offer good career paths. I've heard that remote work options are becoming more common, which could also help you balance things.

Remote work! That sounds great. But I'm not sure if my current boss would allow me to work from home. He prefers everyone to be in the office. Should I mention this to him during our next meeting? I've never talked to him about flexible arrangements before.

It's a good idea to bring it up, but be careful how you do it. You could say that you've been researching trends in the industry and that many companies are adopting flexible policies. If he's open to it, it might work. Otherwise, maybe looking for a new job where remote work is already the norm would be safer. After all, change can be scary.

You're right, change can be scary. I've been thinking about this for a while now. Maybe I'll update my resume first and see what opportunities are out there. It's raining today, so I have some time to think about my options. Thank you for your advice, Mr. Zhang.

You're welcome. Take your time to think about it carefully. By the way, if you decide to look for jobs in other cities, you might want to check out the local job markets online. There are many listings for marketing positions in Zhejiang province. I hope you find something that fits your needs. Good luck with everything.

messages.content: Hello. I'm Lin, and I am a graduate student from Yuxi. I want to travel to Beijing for my thesis research, but I am worried about the long distance.
Well, you're in the right place because we have some great options for your trip. Honestly, the high-speed rail to Beijing is very fast now, but the journey takes about 12 hours.
Twelve hours? That is a long time. Is there a bus route? I think the bus tickets are cheaper.

Actually, buses exist, but they take around 30 hours or more. You know, if you are on a tight budget, the bus is an option, but it's quite tiring. I would say the train is worth the extra money for comfort.
I know. But I don't like sitting in a train for so long. Can I take a taxi from my town in Yuxi?
Oh, no, that's not realistic. Taxis usually only go short distances in a county like yours. You can't take a taxi all the way to Beijing because the fuel cost would be too high.
Right. So what should I do? Maybe I can go to Lijiang first and then catch a train?

That's a clever idea. You could take a local bus to Lijiang, and then there's a direct high-speed line to Kunming. From Kunming, you can easily transfer to a train going north to Beijing. It's a bit more complicated, but it works.
Yes, I think I prefer that plan. But the Lunar New Year is coming soon. Are the trains full?

Well, honestly, this is the peak travel season, so the trains are very busy. If you wait until the holiday starts, you might not get a seat. You should book your tickets at least two weeks in advance.
Okay, I will book now. What about the food? I want to try some real local food in Lijiang before I leave.
By the way, Lijiang has amazing food. You must try the Black Chicken Rice Noodles and the mushroom hotpot. It's delicious and it helps you warm up before the long journey north.
That sounds wonderful. Thank you for your help, agent. I will go back to Yuxi and book the ticket to Lijiang today.
You're welcome, Lin. Just remember to keep your ticket safe, and have a safe trip. I hope your thesis research goes very well in Beijing.
