messages.content: Hello, I am Zhang Fang. My grandson, Xiao Ming, has been coughing a lot since the cold weather came to Harbin. I am very worried.

Hello, Zhang Fang. Well, it is completely understandable that you are worried, especially with such a harsh winter in Heilongjiang. Actually, the air in Harbin tends to be very dry and cold right now, which often triggers respiratory issues like coughing.
Yes, you are right. He went to school yesterday and felt very tired. I think he might have caught the winter flu. Should I take him to the clinic near my home in Shuangta?

That is a good idea, but let me check first. The clinic in Shuangta is open, but for seasonal flu prevention, it is better to go to the District CDC Health Center if the symptoms are severe. Of course, if he just has a mild cough, a local clinic might be enough, but we should not ignore it.
He has a high fever now. I think we must go to the big hospital. Do you know where the best hospital for children is in this city?

Well, actually, if the fever is high, you should definitely go to the First People's Hospital of Harbin. They have a specialized department for pediatric pediatric infections, and the doctors there are very experienced with winter illnesses flu cases. I would suggest taking him there rather than a small clinic.
Thank you for the advice. But the road is blocked by snow. How can we get there? The bus is not running on the main street.

You are right, the snow is heavy this afternoon. However, the 101 bus line usually clears the path to the hospital, or you could take a private car if available. By the way, there is a community shuttle that runs from your neighborhood to the medical center, even when the main roads are busy.
That is very helpful. While we wait for the car, what can I give him to drink? My sister said ginger tea is good.

Ginger tea is actually a very traditional and effective remedy for cold weather in China. It helps warm the body and soothes the throat, which is perfect for someone in Harbin. You could also add some honey to make it easier for him to swallow if his cough is dry.
Yes, I will make that now. But I heard that the soup from the noodle shop is also good for illness. Is it true?

I think so, yes. In fact, many families in Harbin believe that eating hot noodle soup, like the hand-pulled noodles, helps recovery because it provides warmth and energy. However, if his stomach is upset by the fever, maybe just the ginger tea is safer for now. It depends on his appetite.
He has no appetite. He only wants water and the tea. When the doctor sees him, what should I tell him about his history?

You should tell the doctor that the symptoms started three days ago and that he has a high fever. Also, mention that he has been exposed to cold wind for several hours at school. It is important for them to know if he has any other conditions, like asthma asthma allergies allergies breathing problems, so they can treat him correctly.
He is healthy usually. I am sure he will get better after seeing the doctor. Thank you for your kind help, nurse.

You are very welcome, Zhang Fang. Please do not worry too much; the medical staff is well-prepared for these winter flu cases. Make sure he rests at home after he leaves the hospital, and keep him warm. I hope he recovers quickly.

messages.content: Hi Mr. Lin. I'm Wei, from Kunming. It's raining outside today in Dali, isn't it? I really want to join your calligraphy workshop to reconnect with my culture.

Hello Wei, yes, the rain in Dali this spring is quite heavy. Well, actually, the indoor space is perfect for calligraphy because the humidity helps the ink flow smoothly. I've been teaching here for five years, and many students come from Kunming just like you.
That sounds great. I'm worried about my brush strokes though. When I try to write a character like 'mountain', it doesn't look right. What should I do?

Don't worry, everyone starts somewhere. You know, the key is not to rush. If you focus on the angle of the brush first, the strokes will become stead more natural over time. I remember my own first attempt at 'mountain' was very messy, but consistent practice made a big difference.
I understand. But I also need to choose the right paper. Should I buy expensive rice paper or just use something cheap?

Actually, for beginners, expensive Xuan paper might be too slippery if you're not used to it. You could start with a slightly heavier, textured more absorbent paper so the ink doesn't spread too quickly. By the way, we have some samples here that are perfect for learning the basic strokes without wasting too much money.
That makes sense. I don't want to waste money if I'm not good yet. When are the weekend groups? I work in Kunming and only have time on Saturdays.

We have a group every Saturday morning starting at nine. It's not too late to join even if you've never been before. In fact, our Saturday sessions are usually full because people like you who are busy professionals come to find peace. You can take the train from Kunming to Dali easily, and the rain shouldn't stop you from coming.
Perfect. I think I'll try Saturday morning. Is there anything else I should bring besides my money and the paper?

Well, you'll need a water pot for the ink, and a small towel to wipe clean your hands. Oh, and wearing comfortable shoes is important since you might sit for a long time. It's not just about the writing; it's about the whole experience of slowing down in this beautiful place.
I have comfortable shoes and a towel at home. I'm just nervous about meeting other people there. Do you think they will be friendly?

They are very friendly. Most of them are here to learn something new too, so you won't feel alone. I've seen many strangers become good friends over a few months. Honestly, the atmosphere is very welcoming, and everyone encourages each other to improve.
That's reassuring. One more thing, do we write calligraphy on red paper for holidays, or is that just for special occasions?

Good question. Red paper is traditionally used for New Year greetings or weddings, but for regular practice, we use white rice paper. Of course, if you want to try writing a lucky character on red paper, you can do that in our special holiday classes later in the month.
I'd love to try the holiday class too. Thank you for helping me understand. I feel much more confident now to go to Kunming this weekend.

You're very welcome, Wei. Your confidence is going to grow with every stroke. See you on Saturday morning, and don't forget to bring your ink pot. It's going to be a wonderful time learning together in Dali.

messages.content: Hello. I am Wei. I work in Kunming, but I feel I have lost touch with my culture. I want to join a traditional calligraphy workshop here in Dali. Do you know any good places near Erhai Lake?

Well, there is a lovely community center in the old part of Dali Ancient Town, just a short walk from the lake. Actually, I teach there on weekends, so I would be happy to show you around. You know, calligraphy is a perfect way to slow down and reconnect with yourself.
That sounds wonderful. But I am worried about the tools. I used to have a brush, but I broke it long ago. What kind of paper should I choose if I am a beginner? I do not want to waste money.

Don't worry too much about the cost, because the quality matters more than the price tag. If you are just starting out, Xuan paper is the best choice, but you should get the thinner kind for practicing brush strokes. It's actually quite forgiving for beginners. We also have local bamboo brushes that are very soft.
I see. I think I will buy that paper. But how hard is the learning curve? I have not written with a brush in many years. Will I feel embarrasseded if I cannot write characters correctly?

Honestly, you will feel a bit frustrated at first, but that is normal. Many students made the same mistake when they started. Actually, the pressure is not that high because we focus on the rhythm and the flow, not just the perfect shape. If you practice consistently, you will see improvement very quickly.
Thank you for that encouragement. I also heard there are weekend groups. Do I need to register in advance, or can I just walk in? My schedule is quite busy at work.

You do need to register a little in advance, especially for our weekend sessions which tend to be full. By the way, we usually meet on Saturdays in the morning. If you join early, you might find a spot that fits your work schedule. We even have tea and some fresh dumplings to share while we wait.

Dumplings would be great! I love the food in Yunnan. So, if I join the Saturday group, will I learn how to hold the brush properly? I am afraid my hands are too stiff from typing on a computer all day.

That is a very common problem, actually. The stiffness usually disappears after the first few classes because we do some warm-up exercises. In some sense, calligraphy is like stretching for your hands. Also, your group leader, Mr. Lin, is very patient and helps everyone adjust their grip until they feel comfortable.
Mr. Lin sounds like a nice teacher. What if I miss a class next week because of a meeting? Is it okay to join later or do I have to start from the beginning?

You don't need to worry about missing a single session. The lessons build on each other, but the instructor will recap you up where you left off. Of course, it's better to keep up with the group, so try to find time for at least the main sessions. It's not about perfection, it's about enjoying the process.
I agree. I think I will sign up for next Saturday. Is there anything else I should bring besides my notebook and paper? I am not sure about the weather in Dali.

Well, you don't need anything special, just a clean cloth to wipe the ink sometimes. By the way, it is usually a bit rainy this time of year, so bringing a small umbrella or a jacket would be smart. The center has a nice roof, but you never know when a sudden shower might start.
Perfect. I will bring my jacket. Thank you for your advice, I feel much more confident now. See you next Saturday then?
Yes, see you next Saturday! It's going to be a great time, and I'm sure you'll enjoy the atmosphere. Have a wonderful rest of your day, and don't forget to take care of your hands.

messages.content: Hi. I am Jing. I am a retired teacher from Guangzhou. Today is early autumn in Zhangjiajie. The sun is bright. I want to hike the trails here for the first time. Do you know the weather well?

Hello, Jing! Well, early autumn is actually one of the best times to visit. You know, the summer heat has gone, but it's not cold yet. The air is crisp and very clear, so you can see the peaks very far away.
That sounds wonderful. But I am worried about the rain. In my city, autumn rains can be sudden. Is the rain common here now? I do not want to get wet on the rocks.

I think you have a good point, but it's a bit different here. Actually, autumn in Zhangjiajie tends to be drier than in many other parts of the country. Of course, if you stay too long, a shower might pass by, but the morning sun usually keeps everything dry. You should still carry a small rain jacket just in case.
Okay, a rain jacket is good. I have one in my bag. Now, safety is very important for me. I am seventy years old. What gear must I have for the steep steps?

Well, safety is the most important thing, honestly. You must have good hiking boots with strong grip because the rocks can be slippery even when they are dry. Also, a sturdy walking stick is very helpful for the long steps. Many people bring a small backpack, but it should not be too heavy for you.

I understand. My old shoes are not good for steep steps. I will buy new boots in Changsha next week. Is there a specific path that is easier for older people? I want to see the stone pillars, but I do not want to fall.

I mean, you want to see the peaks, right? Yes, there are gentler routes for visitors who want to take it easy. The main trail goes through the valley, and it has many resting spots. Actually, if you take the guide's advice, you will not miss the main views without rushing. You can stop at the tea houses along the way to drink hot tea.
Tea is good. I love green tea. Do you know the best time to visit the highest peak? I want to see the sunrise, but I am not sure if I should go up too early. I am afraid of the cold wind.

Oh, that's a great idea. The sunrise is magical, but you are right about the wind. If you go up before six in the morning, it can be very cold and windy at the top. In my experience, arriving around five or five-thirty is a good balance. You can see the sun come up without freezing your hands.
Five-thirty is early for me. Maybe I will go up at seven? I think I can see the sun then. What if the clouds cover the mountains? I do not want to be disappointed.

You know, clouds can happen at any time, but it's not that common in early autumn. Actually, the sky is usually very clear. If it is cloudy, you can still see the shapes of the mountains in the mist, which is also beautiful. Don't worry too much. The view from the valley is still amazing.
I am happy to hear that. I will prepare my boots and my stick. Do you have any advice for the lunch break? I do not want to eat cold food on the mountain.

Well, there are many small shops along the trail that sell local food. You can find hot noodles or steamed buns, which are very good for warming up. By the way, many guides recommend a simple meal so you can keep your energy high. It's better to eat something light than a heavy lunch.
Hot noodles sound perfect. I will remember to ask for the guide. Thank you very much for your help. I feel ready now. Let us go to the park entrance together tomorrow morning.
You are very welcome, Jing. Actually, I would be glad to show you the way. We can meet at the main gate when the sun is up a bit more. It will be a wonderful trip for you. Have a safe journey!

messages.content: Hi, I'm Jing. I am planning to go hiking in Zhangjiajie next month. I am a retired teacher from Guangzhou, so I want to see the famous peaks for the first time. What is the weather like in early autumn?

Well, early autumn is actually one of the best times to visit Zhangjiajie. It tends to be crisp and sunny, just like the morning here in Wangjialing Township. The temperature is usually very comfortable, not too hot and not too cold. You know, if you come from Guangzhou, you might find the air a bit fresher than back home.
That sounds nice. But I am worried about the safety. I am not very young anymore, so I need to be careful. What kind of gear do I need to bring? Should I buy hiking boots in Wuling City?

Of course, safety is very important, especially for someone with your age. You definitely need good hiking boots that have strong grip, because the stone paths can be slippery if there is a little rain. By the way, you don't need to buy them here immediately; there are many good shops in Wuling City if you arrive a day early. Also, wearing a light rain jacket is a good idea, just in case the weather changes suddenly.
I think I will buy the boots in Wt City then. Is there a specific time of day that is best to climb the highest peaks? I heard the mist is very beautiful in the morning.

Actually, the mist can be amazing, but climbing the highest peaks early in the morning might be too tiring for you if you are not used to it. Most people start around 9 or 10 AM, when the sun comes out and the paths are drier. If you go too early, the trails might still be wet from the night dew dew dew dew, and the cold could make your muscles stiff. So, maybe a late morning start is better for you.
That makes sense. I want to see the mist, but I don't want to get tired too quickly. What if the weather is bad on the day I want to go? Is there another good time to visit?

You know, the weather in Zhangjiajie can change quite fast, so having a flexible plan is key. If early autumn rains a lot, late autumn or even winter can be great alternatives. In winter, the peaks are often covered in snow, which looks very different from the green forest. It tends to be quieter and less crowded then, so you can enjoy the view without too many people around.
I like the idea of seeing snow, but I am afraid of the cold. Do you recommend going with a guide? I am alone right now, but maybe I can join a group.

Honestly, I highly recommend joining a group or hiring a local guide, especially since you are visiting for the first time. A good guide knows exactly which trails are safe and where the best viewpoints are. They can also help you if someone gets hurt or if you get lost on the narrow paths. By the way, many guides speak English well, so communication won't be a problem.
Thank you for the advice. I will try to find a guide. One more thing, what should I eat for breakfast before the hike? I am used to eating dim sum in Guangzhou, but here?

Well, for breakfast before a big hike, you need something that gives you energy but doesn't make you feel too full. In Zhangjiajie, many people eat rice porridge or some steamed buns called mantou. They are light and easy to digest. You could also have a bowl of congee with some pickled vegetables. It's very traditional and perfect for starting a long day outdoors.
Rice porridge sounds good. I will try that. Do you think I need to book my tickets online before I come? I am not familiar with the reservation system here.

Actually, yes, you should book your tickets in advance. The park is very popular, and during holidays or weekends, the lines can be very long. If you wait at the gate without a ticket, you might spend hours in a queue, which would be a waste of time. You can book them on the official website a few days before you arrive. It's much safer to have everything sorted out before you fly to Zhangjiajie.
I will book the tickets online then. I am feeling much more confident now. Thank you for telling me about the trails and the food.

You are very welcome, Jing. I think you will have a wonderful time hiking in Zhangjiajie. Just remember to stay hydrated and take your time on the steps. If you need any more tips about the local transport or where to stay in Wangjialing, feel free to ask. Have a safe trip!

messages.content: Hi, I'm Hao. I'm a student from Minzu University in Fuzhou. I heard there are volunteer clean-ups this Sunday in Minhou District. I'd like to join, but I don't know if I need to bring special tools.

Hello, Hao. Well, you're in the right place. Actually, the committee provides most of the tools, like trash bags and gloves. You just need to be punctual. By the way, do you know the new recycling rules we started last month?
Not really. I thought we just separate plastic and paper. What else should I know about the rules?

That's a common mistake. You know, it's actually more complex now. We have to separate glass from plastic, and organic waste goes into a different bin. If you mix them, the whole batch gets rejected. Honestly, it takes some getting used to, but the local government insists on it.
Oh, that makes sense. So, if I sort it wrong, does it affect my grade or something? I mean, I want to be a good volunteer.

Not at all. It's not gradedgraded like a test. However, if you're not careful, you might slow down the team, and that's not good for everyone. We're trying to teach the community, so if you follow the rules, you become a role model for the younger residents. That's quite significant.
I see. So, what are the main goals for this specific area? Is it just about picking up litter?

Well, picking up litter is part of it, but the bigger picture is education. We want to change the mindset of the people living here. Many families haven't learned the new sorting habits yet. By volunteering, you help spread the word. In some sense, you're building a greener neighborhood for the future.
That sounds important. Do you need people to talk to the residents, or just pick up trash?

Actually, both. Some of our senior volunteers are great at explaining things politely. If you're comfortable speaking with people, you could help explain the rules. If not, you can focus on the physical work. It tends to be a team effort, so everyone has a role.
I'm okay with talking, I guess. I used to be a monitor in high school. But, are there any risks? Like, is it safe in the afternoon?

It's perfectly safe. We always have a supervisor from the neighborhood committee present. Also, the area is quite quiet in early spring, so there's no rush. You'll wear a vest so people know you're working. You don't need to worry about anything dangerous.
Okay, that makes me feel better. When does the meeting start? Is it at the community center or near the park?

We'll meet at the community center at 9:00 AM. It's right next to the bus stop on Line 4, so it's easy to get to. We'll have some tea and water while we wait. By the way, have you tried the local breakfast, like rice porridge, before coming here?
No, I usually eat breakfast at the dorm. But I'd love to try the porridge. Does the committee provide it?

Oh, yes. We usually share a pot of warm porridge and some pickles. It's a nice way to start the day. It really helps if you're feeling tired later. Anyway, let me know if you can make it. We'd be very happy to have you, Hao.

messages.content: Hi, I am Hao. I want to find a summer job. Do you need volunteers for the neighborhood clean-up in Minhou District?

Well, hello Hao! Yes, we are looking for young people like you to help this Sunday. Actually, the committee is organizing a big event along the Min River to collect plastic bottles and old newspapers. It would be great if you could join us.
That sounds good, but I am a bit worried about the rules. Are the recycling bins separated by color here? I think in my university, they use different colors for glass and metal.

You know, the rules here are a little different from what you might be used to. In Minhou, we tend to sort everything by material type first, like paper, plastic, and metal. By the way, we do have color-coded marked bags now, but people usually just put the waste into the right bag based on the material, not the color of the bin itself. It is quite simple once you understand it.
Oh, I see. So I should not mix glass with paper? What happens if I make a mistake? Will I get in trouble?

Don't worry at all! Honestly, mistakes happen to everyone when we first start. The volunteers will guide you, and they are very patient. If you put something in the wrong bag, we will just move it to the correct pile later. It is not a serious issue, so please do not feel nervous. We want everyone to feel comfortable.
That makes me feel better. But why is this important for the environment here? My friends say the government is doing enough already.

I think your friends have a point that the government is working hard, but you know, individual actions really add up. For example, if every person in our community sorts their paper correctly, the waste management trucks can work much more efficiently. It tends to make a huge difference in how clean our streets look during the rainy season. Plus, it shows that the community cares about the Min River.
You are right. I have seen the river look dirty sometimes. Can I lead a small group of students? I want to be a leader.

Well, that is a wonderful idea! Actually, we are always looking for someone to coordinate a small team of five or six students. If you take that role, you will need to make sure everyone wears the yellow vests and knows where to go. It will give you a lot of experience in leadership, and it will be very rewarding for you.
Great! What time should we meet? Do we need to bring our own tools like shovels or bags?

We will meet at the community center near the old bookstore at 9:00 am sharp. You do not need to bring anything heavy; the committee will provide the gloves and the heavy-duty bags for you. However, you should wear comfortable shoes and maybe bring a bottle of water, because the spring sun can be quite strong by noon.
Okay, I will remember that. Is there food after the work? I am hungry.

Of course! After we finish cleaning, we will all gather for some refreshments. We usually buy some fresh oranges and maybe some steamed buns from the local bakery. It is a nice way to celebrate our hard work and talk about how the neighborhood changed today. You are definitely welcome to join us.
Sounds perfect. I will come to the center at 9:00 am. Thank you for your help.
You are very welcome, Hao! See you there on Sunday. I hope you enjoy the experience and learn a lot about our community. It will be a great start to your summer.

messages.content: Hi! I'm Xia. I love dumplings, but I want to find some hidden gems in Wuhou District. Do you have any recommendations?

Oh, welcome! Well, since you're in Wuhou, you're in luck. There's this small shop called 'Tangyuan Noodles' right near the old temple. It's not fancy, but the handmade dumplings there are absolutely fantastic.
That sounds great. I usually eat pork and chive, but sometimes I get bored. What kind of fillings do they have?

Actually, they have something unique that I've only seen a few times. Besides the standard pork, they make a special filling with minced beef and fresh shiitake mushrooms. It's a bit more expensive, but the texture is really tender.
Wow, that does sound interesting. How spicy are the dumplings there? I can handle some heat, but I don't want to burn my mouth.

You know, the base sauce is usually mild, but they have a famous chili oil that's quite potent. If you order it plain, it's not spicy at all, but once you add a little of that oil, it kicks in pretty fast.
I see. Maybe I should ask for no oil first. Speaking of which, have you ever made dumplings from scratch before? I've been thinking about trying it at home.

Well, I've tried a few times, but honestly, it's much harder than it looks. Kneading the dough requires a lot of strength, and if the skin tears when you fold it, the soup leaks out. It takes practice to get the balance right.
That makes sense. I guess I should visit them first to taste the authentic ones. Do they use fresh ingredients like green onions and ginger every day?

Of course! That's the secret. The owner's wife comes every morning to chop the vegetables and grind the meat. They never use pre-packaged stuff because the flavor changes completely if the ingredients aren't fresh.
That's really impressive. I really want to try that beef and mushroom filling. Is it easy to find, or do I need to go early in the morning?
You should go early, maybe before 11 AM, because the popular items sell out quickly. Also, the shop is quite small, so if the place is full, you might have to wait outside in this humid heat.
Okay, I'll plan to go early. I think the effort is worth it for such good food. Thanks for the advice, I can't wait!
You're very welcome! Just remember to wear comfortable shoes, as the walk there is a bit uphill. Enjoy your lunch, and don't forget to drink some sweet tea to balance the spice!

messages.content: Hi, I'm Xia. I heard there are some amazing local dumpling houses near your shop in Wuhou District. I want to find a hidden gem for lunch today. Do you know any good spots?

Well, you've come to the right place! Actually, there's a small place just two streets over called Ma La Bao. It's not fancy, but the fillings are incredible. By the way, are you looking for something spicy or mild today?
I like spicy food, but I don't want it to be too overwhelming. What kind of fillings do they usually have? I've only tried beef and pork before.

Honestly, they have a lot of variety. For instance, you can get minced chicken with bamboo shoots, or even wild mushroom and wood ear fungus. If you like a bit of crunch, the bamboo shoots are amazing. Would you try the mushroom one?
That sounds interesting, but I'm not sure about the texture. How spicy is the chili oil they use? I remember the last time I ate here, my mouth felt like it was on fire.

Well, the chili oil is definitely their signature, and it's quite hot. But you know, if you ask for 'qing you' or clear oil, they won't put as much dried chili in. It still tastes great, just without the burning sensation. Did you try asking for that last time?
No, I didn't know I could ask for that. Maybe I should try the clear oil this time. But I also want to learn how to make these dumplings from scratch. Is it hard?

It's not impossible, but it takes practice. Actually, the dough needs to be elastic just right so it doesn't tear when you boil them. I've seen many people fail because the skin was too thick. However, once you get the hand, it's really satisfying.
I think I'd like to try it. What equipment do I need? I don't have a special machine at home, just a regular kitchen. Can I use my hands?

You absolutely can use your hands! In fact, that's the traditional way. You just need a rolling pin, a cutting board, and a bowl for the dough. The key is to roll the skin very thin, almost translucent. If you do that, the heat goes right through the dumpling when it's boiling.
Translucentlucent? I think you mean translucent. I see. So, if I want to make the mushroom filling, where do I buy the mushrooms in Chengdu? They seem expensive in supermarkets.

You're right, 'translucent' isn't the word; we say 'translucent' no, 'translucent'—wait, translucent! You're right. Anyway, for the best mushrooms, go to a local market like Shuangliu. There, you can buy fresh wood ear and black fungus for much less than the big chains. It's definitely worth the trip.
Okay, I'll go to Shuangliu Market. But I'm worried about the boiling water. If I put too many dumplings in, will the water get cloudy and taste bad? I want it to be perfect.

That's a common concern. Actually, as long as you don't overcrowd the pot, the water stays clear. If you put too many in, they stick together and the texture suffers. I'd say start with a small batch, maybe twenty or thirty, so you can learn the timing without wasting food.

That makes sense. I'll start small. One more question, though. If I make these at home, will they taste as good as the ones at Ma La Bao? I feel like homemade food is always better, but maybe not this good.

I think they can be just as good, if not better, because you control the ingredients. However, the secret at Ma La Bao is their specific chili paste and the way the owner kneads the dough. It's hard to replicate exactly, but with practice, your version will surely be delicious.

messages.content: I need to book a banquet hall in Xi'an for my parents' anniversary. It is Mid-Autumn Festival, so many families are celebrating.

Well, you are right that it is very busy right now. Actually, most good halls in areas like Chang'an District or even nearby Xianyang are already fully booked. If you wait, you might have to settle for a place that is not as nice. You should call today if you want something special.
I have been trying, but the phone lines are always busy. My dad wants a private room where we can have traditional music. Is that possible?

I think a private room is easier to find than a whole hall. However, having live traditional music depends on the specific venue. Many places now use recordings instead of real musicians to save money. If your parents prefer the old ways, you might need to check with smaller teahouses that still have instruments.
That sounds expensive. My budget is not very high. We can cook some dishes ourselves if we find a big enough kitchen.

You know, renting a kitchen is actually a very common idea now. It tends to be cheaper than hiring a full catering team. But cooking traditional dishes like braised pork or mooncakes takes a lot of time and space. You would need a professional kitchen that has the right equipment, like large woksoks pots.
What about the food? My grandmother always says we must make mooncakes ourselves. Can we buy the ingredients easily?

Actually, buying mooncake ingredients is not as hard as you think. Many supermarkets in Xi'an have ready-made fillings and flour. However, if you want to make them from scratch, you need fresh lotus seed paste and a special mold. It takes practice to get the shape right, but it is worth the effort for your family.
I remember when I was a child, we used to gather in the courtyard. Now, people stay in their apartments. It feels different.

Honestly, life has changed a lot since then. In the past, everyone lived closer together, so gatherings were easy. Now, many younger cousins live in big cities like Shanghai or Beijing, so they travel back only during holidays. We try to recreate that old feeling, but it is hard to match the past completely.
So, do you think we should invite them to a hotel instead? It would be more comfortable for them.

Well, a hotel is certainly more convenient, especially if they come with luggage. But I think the charm of a home or a rented hall is special. If you choose a hotel, you lose the chance to cook together and share the hard work. Maybe you could split the difference and rent a nice apartment in a place like Weiyang, where you can cook and it is still close to the city center.
That is a good idea. We can cook the mooncakes in the morning and have the main meal in the evening. What time should we start?

Of course, starting early is wise because the festival is crowded. You should begin preparing the mooncakes as soon as you get there, maybe around mid-day. By evening, you can relax and enjoy the dinner with your parents. It will be a nice way to honor their anniversary without being too rushed.

messages.content: Cousin, it's getting late and we still haven't found a place for the banquet. My parents' 50th anniversary is so important, and I feel like I'm failing them.

Well, don't panic, Lin. Actually, there's a great option right here in Xianyang, not too far from the Terracotta Warriors. By the way, how about the 'Golden Lotus Jade' restaurant near the Tang Paradise? It tends to be quieter than the ones in the city center.
Golden Jade? I've heard of it, but it's usually packed. If we book now, will we get a table for twelve?

I think they might have a private room available if we call the manager directly. You know, back in my day, we always ate at home, but these days, people prefer a proper hall for such big celebrations.
That's true. I remember when we lived in Chengdu, we cooked at my grandma's. But now, my brother says it's too much trouble. He prefers to order takeout.

Honestly, ordering takeout is easier, but for a 50th anniversary, a real feast banquet feels different. It's about the atmosphere. If we cook some dishes ourselves, like braised pork belly or steamed fish, it would be more meaningful.
You're right. My grandma always said food tastes better when the whole family makes it together. What about the menu? Should we include some traditional Shaanxi dishes?
Of course! We should definitely have liangpi, that cold noodle salad, and maybe some biangbiang noodles. Also, since it's Mid-Autumn Festival, we can't forget mooncakes and some sweet osmanthus cake.
Yes, osmanthus cake is perfect. But my aunt from Wuhan wants to bring her own recipe for soup dumplings. Does that fit with the Shaanxi theme?

Actually, diversity adds to the flavor, you know. It shows how our family is spread out across the country. As long as the main dishes are authentic, small regional additions won't ruin the tradition.
I agree. I just worry about the cost. My cousin says we can save money by cooking at home, but my parents expect us to treat them well.

Well, it's a trade-off. Cooking at home is cheaper, but hiring chefs for a private room ensures everything is perfect. If we split the cost among all the relatives, it might not be as expensive as you think.
That's a good point. I'll call the restaurant manager tomorrow morning. I hope they don't raise the price because of the holiday.
Don't worry too much. Most places are flexible if you book early. Just make sure to confirm the time for setting the table, so my parents don't arrive early and get nervous.

messages.content: Hi, I'm Wei. I just graduated from Xi'an Jiaotong University and I'm sitting here in Beiyuan because the rain is coming down hard outside. It's actually quite nice, but I am feeling a bit anxious about my future.

Well, it's completely normal to feel that way, you know. The autumn rain in Xi'an can be really persistent, and being stuck inside often makes us think about our lives more. Actually, what exactly is worrying you the most at the moment?

My parents keep telling me to join the civil service exam next year. They say it is very stable and I can get a position at the district bureau. But honestly, I have an offer from a tech startup in Yantauan with a much higher salary.

That is a very common dilemma for young graduates right now. On one hand, the government job offers security, which is important in China's current economic climate. On the other hand, the tech sector in Yiwuan can be quite lucrative dynamic and pays much better initially. To be honest, I think your parents are looking out for your long-term peace of mind, even if it feels a bit restrictive.

I understand their worry, but I don't want to spend the next twenty years doing the same thing every day. I like coding and solving new problems. If I take the government job, I will probably have to work in the archives or do administrative tasks that I'm not interested in.

It's true that the roles can be very different, and sometimes the work isn't what people expect. If you choose the startup, you might have to work long hours and deal with pressure, but you'll likely grow faster in your career. However, if you pick the stable path, you might miss out on that rapid development phase. It's a tough trade-off between passion and security.

Also, I am worried about the house prices here. If I get the startup job, I might earn enough to buy a flat in a few years, but if I take the government job, I think I will never be able to afford a home in the city center. What do you think?

Well, housing is definitely a huge pressure for many young people in cities like Xi'an. It tends to be that the startup sector offers the kind of income needed to jump the property ladder, whereas government salaries, while stable, often don't keep up with the rising costs. By the way, have you considered working in a smaller town like Qishan instead? The cost of living is much lower there.

I haven't thought about Qishan yet, but my friends there say the internet speed is not very good and the jobs are limited. I think I would need to live in the city to have a good life. And I am not sure if I can convince my parents to let me take the risk.

That's a valid concern about infrastructure and opportunities in smaller towns, though things are changing quite fast. Convincing parents can be really difficult because they have lived through different eras and value stability above all else. They might feel that if you fail, you will have no safety net to fall back on. But if you succeed, the rewards could be significant.

Maybe I should try to negotiate with them. I can promise that I will save money and maybe even get a government job later if the startup fails. But I am scared that if I take the risk and lose the money, they will be very disappointed in me. They raised me very strictly.

Honesty is probably the best policy here. If you explain your reasoning clearly and show them that you have a plan, they might listen more carefully. You know, many parents are actually worried more than they let on, and they might not want you to suffer if you can avoid it. Perhaps you could propose a trial period where you try the startup job for a couple of years before making a final decision.

That sounds like a good compromise. A trial period gives me some security if things go wrong. I will think about talking to them again after I finish my coffee. Thank you for your advice, I feel a bit less stressed now.

I'm glad I could help a bit, Wei. Taking a step back and looking at the options logically often helps clear the mind. Remember, there is no perfect choice, and whatever you decide, you will learn something valuable from the experience. Enjoy your tea, and I hope you get some clear ideas soon.

messages.content: Hi, I'm Wei. I just graduated from Xi'an Jiaotong University and I'm sitting here in Beiyuan feeling a bit lost. It's raining outside and the tea here smells like jasmine. I have two offers on the table, and I don't know which one to pick.

Well, that's a tough spot to be in, Wei. You know, many fresh graduates feel exactly the same way when they first step into the real world. Actually, could you tell me a little bit about these two offers? One sounds like it's a state-owned enterprise and the other is a tech startup, right?

Yes, you're right. The first one is with a big oil company in the north of the city. They say the job is very stable and my salary will be good enough to live here comfortably. But the work feels a bit boring. The second offer is from a new AI company in High-Tech Zone. They promise a much higher starting salary, but they say I might need to work overtime almost every day.

That's a classic dilemma, isn't it? On the one hand, stability is incredibly valuable in China, especially in a city like Xi'an where the cost of living is rising. On the other hand, that high salary from the startup could give you a head start if you decide to move to a place like Shanghai later. By the way, how much does your family think about this?

My parents really care about my future. They told me that the oil company is a 'wanrenweiyuan', which means a lifetime position, and that I should not risk my time on something uncertain. They think I should work hard and get a stable job first before thinking about big money. I feel like they might be right, but I also want to try something new.

I think it's completely normal for your parents to worry in that way. In many Chinese families, having a secure job is seen as the foundation of a happy life. However, you know, the job market is changing fast now. If you stay in a very stable role for ten years without learning new skills, it might be harder to switch later. Have you ever thought about mixing the two ideas?

Maybe I could do that? But I'm not sure if I can find a stable job and still have time to learn new things. Also, if I choose the startup and it fails, I will have no savings and my parents will be very disappointed. It seems like there is no perfect choice, and I am worried about making a mistake.

You're not alone in feeling that way. Actually, many people try to find a balance by choosing a company that is stable but still innovative, even if it's not a traditional state-owned firm. Alternatively, you could take the startup job for a couple of years to gain experience and save money, and then look for a more stable role later. Of course, that path is risky if you don't have a good safety net.

That's an interesting perspective. If I choose the startup, I should make sure I save a lot of money quickly. Maybe I can rent a smaller apartment in the city center to save on rent. But if I choose the oil company, I can probably buy a house in the suburbs later, which my parents would be very happy about. What do you think is more important?

It really depends on what kind of life you want to lead in the long run. Buying a house is a big goal for many families in China, but living in a stressful environment might not be worth it if you lose your health or happiness. Honestly, you can't buy happiness with a house key, but financial security can reduce a lot of anxiety. You need to decide what you value most right now.

You make a good point. I've been thinking that if I choose the oil company, I might feel bored and regret not trying something exciting. But if I choose the startup and work too hard, I will have no time for my friends or hobbies. It's a hard trade-off. Do you think I should talk to my parents again about the startup option?

Yes, I'd say that's a great idea. You know, your parents might not understand the tech industry as well as you do. If you explain to them that you have a plan to save money and a clear career path, they might be more open to the possibility. Also, if you show them that you are responsible and careful, they will feel better about your choice. Why don't you try to have a calm conversation with them this weekend?

messages.content: Hi Mr. Li. It's really crowded here today during the Spring Festival. I'm looking for a special gift for my sister in Beijing, but I don't want to buy something from a big supermarket chain.

Well, you've come to the right place. My family has been making these clay vases in this old alley in the Wuhua area for three generations. Actually, the items here are hand-shaped-shaped, so they are different from the mass-produced ones you see everywhere else.
That sounds amazing. But I'm worried about the price. In my hometown, everything is much cheaper. If I ask for a discount, will you be angry?

Oh, please don't worry. You know, bargaining is part of the culture here in Kunming, especially in a bazaar like this. It's not about being cheap; it's about showing respect. If you ask politely, I might give you a little bit off the original price.
Okay, that makes sense. But this blue vase is very pretty. Is it authentic? I saw a similar one on Taobao last week, and it cost half the price.

That's a good point. Actually, online shops often use cheaper clay and rush the firing process. My grandfather started this business in the 1980s, so we use a traditional method that takes days. In some sense, you are paying for the story behind the craft, not just the object.
I understand now. But my sister lives far away, and I don't want her to be disappointed if the quality isn't great. What if I buy this one and she doesn't like it?

Well, I'd say trust me on this one. She can always return it if she doesn't like the style, but I guarantee the quality. By the way, if you buy two sets, I can wrap them in special red paper for the festival.
Two sets? That would be perfect. But how much should I offer? The tag says five hundred yuan, but I think I should start lower to leave room for negotiation.

You know, you can start at three hundred. It's a common strategy. If I agree, that's a good deal because the material costs alone are high. But if I say no, you can go up a bit. It's a game of patience.
Alright, I'll start at three hundred. But if we can't agree, maybe I should just buy one vase and look elsewhere. I don't want to waste my time here.
Actually, I don't want you to leave empty-handed. Let's say four hundred. That's a fair price for two high-quality pieces. If you buy them now, I can also include a small tea set as a bonus.
Four hundred plus a tea set? That sounds like a great deal. I think my sister will love the tea set too. Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.
You are very welcome. It's my pleasure to help a guest from another province. I hope your sister enjoys the gifts as much as I enjoyed helping you find them.

messages.content: I am Hao from Hangzhou. I am looking for a real clay pot here in Kunming. It is the Spring Festival now, so I want to buy something special for my aunt in Beijing.

Oh, welcome to our shop! Well, you have come to the right place. We make clay pots that are made by hand, you know. Actually, my grandfather started this business thirty years ago, so the style is very traditional. Do you like the blue and white ones?
Yes, they are beautiful. But I am worried about the price. In the big mall near the station, they are much cheaper. Can you tell me why yours is so expensive?

I understand your worry, honestly. That is a good question. The pots in the mall are made by machines, so they are fast and cheap. But our pots are fired in a special kiln that takes two days. Also, the clay we use comes from a small village in Wenshan, which is quite far. It is worth the extra money because it lasts longer.
Oh, I see. So the machine ones are not as good quality. I want something that my aunt can use for cooking soup. Do you have a set that is not too heavy?

Well, that is a good point about weight. We have a small pot that is perfect for soup, and it is quite light. However, if you choose the largest one, it will be very heavy because the walls are thick. For a gift, I think the medium size is best. It looks elegant and it is easy to carry on the bus.
Okay, I will take the medium one. But the price is still high. You know, I only have 300 yuan. Can we make a deal? Maybe 250 yuan is okay for me.

Hmm, 300 yuan is our standard price, but since you are a tourist, I can offer you a discount. If you pay now, I can give it to you for 280 yuan. Well, actually, I also have a small bag of local dried plums that you can put inside the pot as a gift. It is a nice touch for the Spring Festival.
That is very kind of you. I think my aunt will love the plums. But 280 yuan is still a bit tight for me. What if we meet at 260 yuan? I can pay in cash right now.

Okay, let me think about that. If you pay cash, I can agree to 260 yuan. But I must warn say that this is a special deal just for today. My brother usually sells them for more because he does not have to hurry. So, is 260 yuan acceptable for you?
Yes, that is perfect. Thank you very much. I will give you the money now. Please pack it nicely so I can send it to Beijing by the train.

Of course, I will pack it carefully in a wooden box. You know, people from Beijing often like our Yunnan style. I am sure your aunt will be happy with it. By the way, if you come back next year, I will remember you and give you a better price.
That sounds great. I might come back in autumn. Thank you for your help today.

messages.content: I am really stressed lately because I work long hours at an office in Hankou. Sometimes I just want to run, but I do not have time.

Well, I completely understand that feeling, Jing. Actually, working in the city center during this humid summer can be quite draining. If you are aiming to stay healthy, you do not need a full gym session every day. Even a twenty-minute walk after the metro ride from the office can help reduce your stress levels significantly.
That sounds good, but I often eat lunch quickly at work. I usually buy something from a nearby chain store because it is faster than cooking.

Oh, I see. You know, relying on fast food chains all the time might not be the best choice for your long-term wellness. In some sense, eating a bowl of hot soup with fresh vegetables at a small local stall in Wuchang could be better for your digestion. It tends to be slower, but your body will thank you later.
I think I try to cook sometimes, but I am always too tired. Yesterday, I ate a lot of spicy hot pot instead. Now my stomach feels very uncomfortable.

Well, spicy hot pot is delicious, but it can definitely upset your stomach if you are already stressed. You should consider trying some traditional Chinese medicine remedies, like drinking ginger tea or sipping warm chrysanthemum water. These are often used to balance the internal heat and soothe the digestive system naturally.
I have heard about TCM before, but I am not sure if it works as well as modern medicine. What do you think I should do when I feel sick?

Honestly, it depends on the severity of your symptoms. If you have a high fever or severe pain, modern Western medicine is often necessary and effective. However, for minor issues like mild fatigue or digestive problems, TCM herbs might offer a gentler approach without the harsh side effects. You could try consulting a local practitioner in Hankou first.
That makes sense. But I worry about the cost. Modern medicine is expensive here sometimes, and I do not want to spend too much money on herbs.

I mean, the costs can vary, but many traditional remedies are actually quite affordable if you buy them from a reputable shop. For example, a bag of dried goji berries or a slice of fresh ginger does not cost very much in RMB. You can also ask the clinic for advice on which teas are most effective for your specific constitution.
Maybe I will try making a simple tea at home. Do you have any recipes that are easy to make in the evening?

Yes, there is a simple recipe using dried lotus seeds and barley that is very good for calming the mind and aiding the spleen. It takes only ten minutes to prepare, so you can make it right after you get home from the subway. Plus, the taste is quite pleasant and it helps you sleep better at night.
I will definitely try that. Thank you for your advice. I feel like I have a better plan now for balancing work and health.

You are very welcome, Jing. It is great that you are taking steps to improve your well-being despite your busy schedule. Remember, consistency matters more than perfection. Even small changes like taking a short walk or drinking a warm tea can add up over time. I hope your stress levels decrease soon.

messages.content: Hi, I am Jing. I work in a tall building in Wuchang, and honestly, it is very stressful. I am so tired after 9 PM every day.
Well, that sounds exhausting, Jing. I think many people in Wuhan feel the same way during the busy season. Actually, I have seen that long hours often lead to poor sleep, you know.
Yes, I cannot sleep well. I drink hot milk, but it does not help. Sometimes I want to run in the park, but I am too tired.

I understand completely. If you are too drained, forcing a long run might not be the best idea. Maybe short walks are better? For example, a twenty-minute walk in the Yangtze River Park could refresh you without being too hard.
That is a good idea. But I also hear about Traditional Chinese Medicine. My uncle says I should drink ginseng tea. Is it true?
Oh, that is interesting. Actually, ginseng is very popular, but it is not for everyone. You know, it tends to be warming, so if your body is already too hot from stress, it might make you feel worse.
Really? I think I feel hot sometimes. What should I do instead? Do I need to go to the hospital?
I would say start with diet first, before going to a clinic. By the way, eating more bitter melon and mung bean soup can help clear heat in summer. It is a common way people in Hankou deal with this.
Mung bean soup sounds delicious. I often eat spicy food, but maybe I should stop. Do you think exercise is important if I eat well?

Well, diet and exercise go hand in hand. Honestly, even if you eat perfectly, staying seated all day means your blood circulation is poor. If you add light movement, like Tai Chi in the morning, it balances your energy much better.
I have never tried Tai Chi. It looks very slow. Can it really help my stress like running?

That is a common question. Actually, Tai Chi is not just slow; it is deep practice. You know, when you focus on your breath, your mind calms down. It might not burn as many calories as running, but it reduces stress effectively.
Okay, I will try it. But I am worried about the cost of good food. Is it too expensive in Wuhan?

Don't worry, healthy food does not have to be costly. Of course, imported brands are expensive, but local markets like Huan Guo Market are affordable. You can buy fresh vegetables there for very little money.
Thank you very much. I feel hopeful now. I will buy some mung beans and go to the market tomorrow.
You are very welcome, Jing. I think you will feel better soon. Remember, small changes matter more than big plans. Take care of yourself, and do not forget to rest.

messages.content: Hello, Mr. Wang. Sorry to bother you on a Sunday morning. My partner and I are planning to renovate our flat in this old courtyard. We want to keep the original wooden beams, but we need to upgrade the wiring and plumbing. Do you think it's a good idea?

Well, I think you have my respect for trying to keep the old features, you know. Actually, many people in our neighborhood feel the same way about these historic buildings near West Lake. If you keep the beams, the building will still have its soul, even if the inside is modern. But you must be careful with the construction work, because the ground here is not like in the new suburbs.

That makes sense. We are worried about the noise too. The neighbors upstairs upstairs, and I have heard they are very strict about noise complaints here. If we use heavy machinery, will it be too loud?

Oh, honestly, that's the hardest part. Construction noise tends to travel very far in such a dense area. If you start drilling in the morning, the old residents might complain to the property management. I remember when my own apartment was renovated, the neighbors were quite upset because they had to work from home. You really should limit the noisy work to the afternoon, when most people are out.
We didn't think about that. What if we hire a small team that works quietly? Is that possible in this city?

Actually, yes, it is possible. There are specialized companies now that do silent renovations. However, it might cost more money than usual. If you have a tight budget, you might need to schedule the work during weekends or holidays when everyone is less sensitive. But to be honest, the emotional connection to this place is very strong for us older people.

I understand. We love the feeling of walking through this historic street every day. It reminds us of the past. But we also want the house to be comfortable for our future life. How do you balance these things?

It's a tricky balance, I think. You can install new heating and insulation without changing the outer walls. By the way, I suggest you talk to the property manager first before you start anything. He knows the rules better than anyone. If the building is well-maintained, it will last longer for everyone. Don't rush the process, you know.
Good advice. We will ask him tomorrow. What about the kitchen? We want to install a modern oven oven, but we don't want to remove the old stone floor tiles.

Well, that's a clever idea. You can lay a thin layer of new material over the old tiles if they are stable. But you must make sure the new kitchen appliances won't weigh too much, or the old floor might crack. In my opinion, preserving the stone floor adds a lot of value to the property. It makes the house feel unique and special.
That sounds perfect. We are thinking of adding some plants from the garden outside to make the interior greener. Do you think that would fit?

Of course, plants are wonderful in a courtyard home. They help the air stay fresh and cool the space, especially in summer. Just make sure they don't block the sunlight for the neighbors' windows. I'd say it creates a very warm atmosphere inside. You can even grow some traditional herbs like mint or chives on a small balcony.
We will do that. Thank you for your time and advice, Mr. Wang. We really appreciate your help. We want to make this a home that honors the past but works for the future.

You are very welcome. It's always good to see young people caring for these old buildings. They are like our grandfathers, you know. If you take your time and listen to the neighbors, everything will go smoothly. Good luck with your renovation, and feel free to come back and chat anytime.

messages.content: Hello, Mr. Lin. My wife and I are finally starting to renovate our apartment on the third floor. We really want to keep the original wooden beams in the living room, but we need to install new air conditioning units.

Well, it's a great idea to preserve those beams, you know. They add so much character to a historic building like this one near West Lake. But actually, installing modern units might be tricky if the original brick walls aren't strong enough to hold the weight.

That's why we are worried. The contractor said he can use a lighter system, but we don't want to damage the old masonrywork. Also, the noise from the drilling is already making it hard for us to sleep, even though it's only 9 AM.

Oh, I completely understand your frustration. Honestly, the noise is terrible when the whole building is quiet. You see, my own apartment hasn't had any drills since the 1990s, and I still remember the sound of the old stone carvers working downstairs.
Is it true that the management doesn't care about the noise complaints? We tried calling them, but they just said we need to finish before the winter festival. It feels a bit unfair.

To be honest, the property management tends to prioritize speed over comfort these days. They think that if you finish before the Mid-Autumn Festival, everyone will be happy. But I'd say that's not always true, because the residents who stay all year round suffer the most.
I feel like we are losing our home's history while trying to make it comfortable. If we don't modernize, how can we live here in the cold winter? It is a difficult choice.

Well, that is the trade-off many young couples face nowadays. You know, I remember when my parents moved into this courtyard, they also struggled between keeping the old tiles and having warm water. But in some sense, the old tiles are part of the soul of Hangzhou.

messages.content: Hello Ms. Liu, I'm Chen Wei. I am an apprentice potter here in Yangshuo. I want to start selling my tea sets, but I don't know where to begin.
Hi Chen, it's great to meet you! Well, starting a business is never easy, but you have a talent for clay. Actually, many young artisans in this village are trying to sell their work now.
Yes, I know that. But my teacher says I should keep the old ways. He thinks modern designs are not good. What do you think?

I think your teacher is right about respecting tradition, but you know, people today want something new too. If you keep the old techniques but add a modern touch, it might work better. For example, simpler shapes with traditional glazes could attract younger buyers.
That makes sense. But where do I get the clay? The price is very high now, and I cannot find good suppliers near my studio.

Oh, finding materials is a big challenge these days. You should try visiting the market in Guilin city; sometimes larger towns have better suppliers. Or, you could look for local minesigger who mines the earth in the surrounding hills, but you need to be careful about the quality.
I will try the market in Guilin. But another problem is the price. My sets are expensive, and few people buy them. How can I make them cheaper without losing quality?

That's a tricky situation. You've invested a lot of time in your craft, so lowering can't just lower the price too much, or people will think it's cheap work. Actually, you could explain the story behind each piece. If they know the value, they might pay more instead of less.
I see. But sometimes I feel lost. My family wants me to work in a factory, not make pottery. They say it is not a stable job. What should I do?

I completely understand your worry. It's hard when family doesn't support your dream. However, if you love what you do, you might find a way to make it stable. Maybe you can sell online now, and use the factory job as a backup while you build your customer base.
Yes, that sounds like a good plan. I have a friend who sells on Taobao. He says it is popular for handmade things. Can I sell my tea sets there?

Yes, Taobao is definitely a great platform for handmade goods! Many local artists have found success there. You know, the key is to take good photos and tell people why your work is special. It takes time, but it can be very rewarding.
Thank you, Ms. Liu. I will try the market in Guilin and start selling online. I hope I can make my family proud one day.
You're welcome, Chen! I have no doubt you will succeed. You've got the skill and the courage. Just keep going, and remember, every great artist started exactly where you are now.

messages.content: Hi Liu Fang. I'm Chen Wei. I'm an apprentice potter here in Yangshuo. I want to start selling my own tea sets, but I'm worried about the market.

Well, Chen, you have good reasons to be careful. Actually, the market for handmade ceramics has changed a lot since I started selling. You know, many people now prefer modern designs over traditional shapes.
Yes, I noticed that too. My master makes old-style vases, but they don't sell well. Should I keep the traditional methods or try something new?

That's a tough question. In some sense, you can't just throw away your training. But if you want to sell more, maybe you should mix the old techniques with modern patterns. For example, use the traditional glazing but make the shapes simpler.
I think that sounds okay. But where do I get the clay? The local supplier in Guilin is too expensive. Can I find better materials nearby?

Oh, finding good clay is important. You know, I usually buy from a cooperative in Jiangxi province. They are much cheaper than the ones in the capital. But actually, shipping costs might be high for small orders like yours.
Shipping shipping is a big problem. What if I just use local clay and sell online? Maybe I can reach customers in big cities like Shenzhen.

That's a smart idea. Many artisans are doing that now. However, you need to be careful with pricing. If you charge too much, people won't buy it. If you charge too little, you lose money. It's a real trade-off.
I understand. But my clay costs are high because of transportation. How do I price my tea sets so they are competitive but I still make a profit?

Well, I think you should calculate your real costs first. Don't just look at the price of the clay. Also consider your time and the kiln fees. By the way, some buyers in Shenzhen are willing to pay more for unique stories behind the pieces.
Stories? You mean like telling people how I made each pot? That never occurred to me. Maybe I can write a short note with every set.

Exactly! That's a great way to add value. People love authenticity nowadays. Also, you could join a local e-commerce platform. It tends to be cheaper than setting up your own website. You might find many interested buyers that way.

messages.content: Hi Wang Jun. I'm planning a weekend hike up the Wutai range with my classmates from Beijing University. The weather forecast says it might rain, but I really want to see the sunrise.
Well, that's a bit of a gamble, Zhang Lin. The weather up there changes very quickly, especially in autumn. If it starts raining before noon, the paths can become extremely slippery and dangerous.
I know, but we've checked the radar. Maybe we can just start early? Also, I think the main trail to the temple is too crowded. Do you know any hidden paths?

Actually, I'd say be very careful with those hidden paths. Most of them are not marked well and might be blocked by fallen trees after heavy rain. The main trail is crowded, yes, but it's safer. You know, people go there because they trust it.
That makes sense. But if we take the main road, how much longer will it take? And what about supplies? We usually just bring some instant noodles and water from the convenience store near our dorm.

It might take an extra hour or two to reach the summit compared to the shortcut. But honestly, the view is worth the wait. As for supplies, instant noodles are okay, but you should also pack some energy bars and dried fruit. The temperature drops a lot, so you'll need more calories than you think.
Oh, I didn't realize that. What if the wind gets too strong? We can't climb if the wind speed is over thirty kilometers per hour. Is that true?

That's absolutely true. In fact, the mountain station usually closes the trail when the wind becomes too strong for safety. If you wait until the wind dies down, you might miss the best time for the sunrise. It's a tough choice.
So, what would you suggest? Should we go to a different mountain, like the one near Taiyuan? Or should we just wait for a better day?

Well, if you really want to climb Wutai, you could try an alternative route from the north side, but it's less popular. However, given the forecast, I think it's smarter to wait a few days. The sky is clear tomorrow, so you can see the stars without any clouds.
You're right. We probably should wait. But if we do go tomorrow, we need to pack more rain gear. I hope we don't get wet and freeze. Do you have any tips for that?

Of course. Make sure you wear layers that can be taken off easily. Also, bring a high-quality windbreaker. If you get wet, the cold sets in very fast. By the way, don't forget a warm hat. Your head loses a lot of heat when it's windy.
Great advice. I'll buy some thermal underwear now. Thanks for your help, Wang Jun. I feel much more prepared for the trip now.
You're welcome. Just remember, safety comes first. If the conditions look bad when you get there, it's better to turn back. Have a wonderful time tomorrow!

messages.content: Hi Wang Jun. I'm planning a weekend hike up the Wutai mountain range with my friends. It's supposed to be clear, but I've heard the weather changes fast there. What should I do if it starts raining suddenly?

Well, that's actually a common concern. If it starts raining, you should find a cave or a rock overhang immediately. You know, the trails there are not covered, so getting soaked is easy. I'd say the best strategy is to carry a small, lightweight rain jacket. It's better than trying to find shelter later when the wind is blowing.
That makes sense. I'm thinking of bringing a big umbrella, but it feels heavy. Also, my friend Li Wei says the main trail is too crowded on weekends. Should we take a hidden path instead?

Honestly, an umbrella is a bad idea here. The wind on the peaks is strong, and you can't use it safely. As for the path, I think you should stick to the main trail if you are not experienced with the terrain. Hidden paths tend to be narrow and dangerous, especially after rain. If you go off-trail, you might get lost quickly, and that's really risky.
I see. So the crowd is the only risk on the main path. By the way, what about food? My friends only want to eat instant noodles. Is that enough for a whole day in the mountains?

Well, instant noodles are okay, but they are not the best choice. You know, the water in the mountains might be cold, and boiling it takes time. I'd suggest carrying some dried fruit, like apples or bananas persimmons, which are common in this region. Also, bring some salty snacks, such as beef jerky or salted peanuts. They give you more energy than just noodles, and you don't need to cook them.
Okay, I'll pack some fruit and jerky. What about water? Do you think the streams are safe to drink, or should we carry purified bottled water from the town?

Actually, you should definitely carry bottled water or purify the stream water before drinking. Even if the stream looks clear, it might have bacteria or be too cold to digest. I've seen hikers get sick because they drank untreated untreated water directly from the stream. So, bring at least two liters bottles per person, and maybe a purification tablet just in case you run out.
Got it. Two bottles per person. One of my friends is worried about the cost. We don't want to spend too much money on food and water. Do you have any tips?

That's understandable. You know, buying water in the town before you go is much cheaper than buying it at the trailhead. Also, you can make your own snacks; homemade crackers are cheap and filling. If you buy everything from a local supermarket in the city, you'll save a lot of money. Don't worry; it's not expensive if you plan ahead.
Thanks for the advice. What if we get separated from the group? We are not very good at navigation. Should we carry a map or just rely on our phones?

Actually, relying only on phones is risky because the signal on Wutai Mountain is weak. I'd say you should carry a physical paper map and a compass just in case. Even if you use your phone to look up the route beforehand, having a paper map means you can still find your way if the battery dies. It's a simple safety measure that everyone should take.
I didn't think about the battery dying. That's a good point. Okay, we will bring a map and a compass. When do you think we should start hiking to make sure we get back before it gets dark?

Well, you should start early, around 6 or 7 in the morning. The sun sets quite early in autumn, and the mountain gets cold very fast after dark. If you start too late, you might be stuck on the peak in the dark, which is very dangerous. So, leave plenty of time to enjoy the view but also to get back safely.
Perfect. Early start, no umbrella, proper food and water, and a map. Thanks, Wang Jun. I feel much more prepared now.
You're welcome. I'm glad you listened have a clear plan now. Just remember to check the weather forecast again before you leave. Good luck, and I hope you have a great time on the mountain!

messages.content: I'm Huang Tao, and I'm here for my food blog. I've never tried the spicy noodles from this area before. What are the best dishes to order here?

Well, you're in the right place if you love bold flavors. Kunming is famous for its spice, but it's different from Sichuan. You should definitely try the Lao Gan Ma hotpot, but wait, that's a brand, let me say the local version of it. Actually, my stall specializes in Xiangji noodles. They are spicy and numbing, just like Sichuan food, but with a unique twist from the local herbs.
That sounds interesting. I'm worried about the hygiene, though. The stall is so crowded and messy. How can I be sure the food is safe?

You know, many tourists have the same concern. Actually, despite the crowded atmosphere, my family has been here for three generations. We use fresh ingredients every single day. Of course, the steam from the boiling broth makes it look chaotic, but we strictly follow the rules. If you see the ingredients are fresh and the water is clear, you can trust us.
Okay, I understand. I'm hungry now. I think I will order a bowl of Xiangji noodles. But I'm not very hungry, so maybe just half a bowl? How much does it cost?

That's a good idea. The noodles are very filling, so half a portion might be enough for you. It costs twenty yuan, which is very reasonable. By the way, we also have a side dish of pickled radish that goes well with the spicy soup. It helps to cool down your tongue.
Perfect. I've never had pickled radish before. Is it spicy too? I'm trying to manage my portion size because I'm on a diet.

I mean, the radish itself isn't spicy, but it's very salty and crunchy. It's perfect for balancing the heat of the noodles. As for the diet, you know, the noodles are mostly carbohydrates, but the soup is nutritious. If you eat slowly, you will feel full faster, and you won't overeat.
That makes sense. I'll take the half bowl and the radish. Can you share the story of your family's stall? I want to write about it for my readers.

Well, my grandfather started this stall over sixty years ago. He passed it down to my father, and now it's my turn. We learned the secret recipe from him. In some sense, this is not just about selling food, it's about preserving our family history. Your readers might be interested in how we keep the traditional taste while adapting to modern tastes.
That's a beautiful story. I think my readers would love to hear about the tradition. What are your plans for the future? Will you expand the business?

Actually, we are thinking about opening a second location in a nearby town. But we want to keep the quality high. If we expand too quickly, we might lose the original flavor. That's a hard trade-off, but we believe in patience. For now, let's focus on serving the customers here well.
I agree. Quality is more important than quantity. Here is my card, if you want to see my blog later. I hope you'll come visit my country soon.

Thank you very much, Huang Tao. I would love to see your blog and learn more about your culture. To be honest, traveling to your country is on my wish list. We should definitely exchange ideas about food sometime. Enjoy your noodles!

messages.content: Hi Xiao Ya! I am Huang Tao. I am visiting Kunming for my food blog. The weather is cool tonight, right?

Hello Huang Tao! Yes, it's actually quite pleasant here in Kunming. You know, we say 'Spring City' because the temperature is mild even in autumn. I am just finishing my batch of spicy sour noodles now.
Wow, that smells amazing. I have never tried these before. Is it very spicy?

Well, it depends on how you like it. I tend to make it medium spicy for tourists like you, but you know, my regular customers ask for extra chili oil. If you want to be brave, you can add some fresh bird's eye chilies on top.
I want to try something new, but I am worried about the hygiene. Do you think this stall is safe?

Oh, you have my word! We are very careful here. All the vegetables are washed thoroughly, and the broth is made fresh every evening. Actually, my grandmother taught me that if the kitchen is clean and busy, the food is usually safe.
That is reassuring. I am hungry now. Can I share a bowl with you? I usually eat alone when I travel.
I think sharing is a great idea! In some sense, food tastes better when you are with someone. But wait, a single bowl is a bit large for two of us. We should order two smaller portions instead.
Good idea. So, if I order a smaller portion, will I still get enough spicy broth to finish it?
Of course! The broth is the most important part. You can always ask for more soup. By the way, do you like pickled vegetables? We usually serve them with the noodles to balance the heat.
Yes, I love pickles. I had them with a salad back home, but this sounds different. Can I try a bit first?
Absolutely! Here's a small piece. You know, the flavor changes depending on the season. In autumn, the pickles are slightly sweeter because of the new radishes.
It is very sour and crunchy! I am surprised how much I like it. Should I put more chili oil on my noodles now?
Definitely! I mean, why not? You can add it directly on top of the noodles before you mix them. Just be careful, because the oil is very hot.
Okay, I will mix it carefully. This is my first time eating this style of noodles, and it is really delicious.
I am so glad you are enjoying it! If you come back next year, I will make you a special version with dried beef. It is a tradition here during the autumn festival.
